concepts.name: Linear equation
concepts.statement: A linear equation in the unknowns x₁, x₂, …, xₙ may be written in the form a₁x₁ + a₂x₂ + … + aₙxₙ = b, where a₁, a₂, …, aₙ are real numbers known as coefficients; we also say that x₁, x₂, …, xₙ are the variables in the equation. Each term on the left is the product of a constant and the first power of an unknown, so the equation of any line can be expressed in the form ax + by = c, vertical lines such as x = 3 included.

forms.condition: the equation of a line, two unknowns

concepts.name: System of linear equations
concepts.statement: By a system of linear equations, or a linear system, we mean a set of linear equations written in a common set of unknowns.

concepts.name: Solution of a linear system
concepts.statement: A solution to a linear system is simply a set of numbers x₁ = s₁, x₂ = s₂, …, xₙ = sₙ that satisfy all the equations in the system; to check that (x, y) = (2, 3) is a solution of a system, we verify that each of its equations is true at those values.

concepts.name: Solution space
concepts.statement: We call the set of all solutions the solution space of the linear system. For equations in two unknowns it is seen graphically as the points where the lines of the equations meet; in three unknowns, where the planes meet.

concepts.name: Solutions to sets of linear equations
concepts.statement: Given a set of linear equations, there are either infinitely many points, exactly one point, or no points that satisfy every equation in the set. This is a general principle to which we will frequently return.

concepts.name: Solution sets as lines and planes
concepts.statement: The solutions to a linear equation in two unknowns form a straight line, and the solutions to a linear equation in three unknowns form a plane, such as y = 0 in the plane and z = 0 in space. The solution space of a set of equations is the intersection of these lines or planes: two planes typically meet in a line and three planes in a point, though in special cases two planes are parallel or three planes have no common point.

concepts.name: More equations, fewer solutions
concepts.statement: A single equation has infinitely many solutions; as we add equations, we add conditions, which lead to a smaller number of solutions, and eventually there are too many equations and no point satisfies all of them. So we come to expect that more equations than unknowns give no solutions and fewer equations than unknowns give infinitely many, though there are exceptions: two equations in two unknowns may be parallel lines with no solution, and three equations in two unknowns may have a single solution.

concepts.name: Recognizing a linear equation
concepts.statement: Deciding whether an equation is linear: it is linear when it can be rewritten with each term the product of a constant and the first power of an unknown, as x = 3z − 4y can be written x + 4y − 3z = 0, and it is not linear when a term such as xy or y² appears.

concepts.name: Checking a solution of a linear system
concepts.statement: Checking whether a set of values is a solution of a linear system by substituting it into every equation and verifying that each equation is true; a set of values that fails even one equation is not a solution, and finding more than one solution suggests there are infinitely many.

concepts.name: Gaussian elimination
concepts.statement: Gaussian elimination is our primary tool for describing the solution space of a linear system. Using replacement and scaling operations we eliminate the first variable from all but one equation and proceed to the next variables working left to right until the system is triangular, then use back substitution moving right to left until it is decoupled. On the augmented matrix, the same scaling, interchange, and replacement operations construct the one reduced row echelon matrix that is row equivalent to it, and the process of constructing this matrix is called Gaussian elimination.

concepts.name: Decoupled system
concepts.statement: A linear system in which each equation has only one variable, so that it prescribes a specific value for that variable, is called decoupled; such a system has exactly one solution, which can be read off the equations.

concepts.name: Triangular system
concepts.statement: A system such as x + 2y − 2z = −4, −y + z = 3, 3z = 3 is called a triangular system due to the shape formed by its coefficients: each equation involves fewer of the leading variables than the one above it.

concepts.name: Back substitution
concepts.statement: Triangular systems are easily solved by back substitution: the last equation gives the value of the last variable, which is substituted into the equations above it to obtain a new system having the same solutions; repeating this moves through the variables right to left and arrives at a decoupled system, which shows there is exactly one solution.

concepts.name: Scaling, interchange, and replacement
concepts.statement: Three operations transform a system of linear equations into a new system of equations having the same solution space. Scaling: we can multiply one equation by a nonzero number. Interchange: interchanging equations will not change the set of solutions. Replacement: we may multiply one equation by a real number and add it to another equation. Each can be reversed, which is why the solution space is the same; on an augmented matrix they act on the rows.

concepts.name: Matrix
concepts.statement: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers, such as the array that records the numerical data of a linear system once we forget about the variables; its rows are what scaling, interchange, and replacement act on, and a matrix with three rows and five columns is a 3 × 5 matrix.

concepts.name: Augmented matrix
concepts.statement: When writing a linear system, we always write the variables in the same order in each equation; we then construct an augmented matrix by simply forgetting about the variables and recording the numerical data in a rectangular array. The vertical line reminds us where the equals signs appear in the equations, and the entries to its left are the coefficients of the equations.

concepts.name: Coefficient matrix
concepts.statement: We sometimes choose to focus only on the coefficients of the system, in which case we write the coefficient matrix: the entries of the augmented matrix to the left of the vertical line, without the column of constants.

concepts.name: Row equivalence
concepts.statement: The symbol ∼ between two matrices indicates that they are related by a sequence of scaling, interchange, and replacement operations; since these operations act on the rows of the matrices, we say the matrices are row equivalent. The linear systems corresponding to two row equivalent augmented matrices have the same solution space.

concepts.name: Leading entry
concepts.statement: If we move across a row of a matrix from left to right, the first nonzero entry we encounter is the leading entry in the row.

concepts.name: Reduced row echelon form
concepts.statement: A matrix is in reduced row echelon form if: when the entries in a row are all zero, the same is true of any row below it; the first nonzero entry in each row, its leading entry, is 1; the leading entry in any row is to the right of the leading entries in all the rows above it; and a leading entry is the only nonzero entry in its column. We call a matrix in reduced row echelon form a reduced row echelon matrix, whether it is an augmented matrix or a coefficient matrix.

concepts.name: Uniqueness of the reduced row echelon form
concepts.statement: For any given matrix, there is exactly one reduced row echelon matrix to which it is row equivalent. There is a sequence of row operations that transforms any matrix into one in reduced row echelon form, and the conditions that define reduced row echelon matrices guarantee that this matrix is unique.

concepts.name: Free variable
concepts.statement: When the equations of a reduced row echelon matrix place no restriction on the value of a variable, so that we obtain a solution for any value of it, we call it a free variable; the presence of a free variable means the linear system has infinitely many solutions.

concepts.name: Basic variable
concepts.statement: The variables that are determined once we make a choice of the free variables are called basic variables.

concepts.name: Parametric description
concepts.statement: A description of the solution space in which the basic variables are written in terms of the free variables, such as x = −1 − 2z, y = 2 − z, is called a parametric description of the solution space.

concepts.name: Reading the solution space from a reduced row echelon matrix
concepts.statement: Describing the solution space from the reduced row echelon form of an augmented matrix: write the linear system it corresponds to; an equation 0 = 0 imposes no restriction and is ignored; an equation 0 = 1 is not true for any values, so there is no solution; otherwise write the basic variables in terms of the free variables, which gives a unique solution when there is no free variable and infinitely many when there is one.

concepts.name: Computing in Sage
concepts.statement: Sage uses the standard operators +, -, *, / and ^ for the usual arithmetic operations. Commands on separate lines are evaluated in turn and only the result of the last is displayed unless print is used; the result of one command may be given a name and referred to in a later command. Sage is written in Python, and Python code may be entered into a Sage cell.

concepts.name: Entering a matrix in Sage
concepts.statement: A matrix is created in Sage by matrix(m, n, [entries]), whose three arguments are the number of rows, the number of columns, and the entries listed by row inside square brackets, separated by commas; or by listing its rows, matrix([[…], […]]). There is no way of specifying whether a matrix is augmented or a coefficient matrix, so it is up to us to interpret the results.

concepts.name: Finding a reduced row echelon matrix in Sage
concepts.statement: Giving a matrix a name, A = matrix(…), its reduced row echelon form is found by A.rref(). If all the entries are integers, Sage computes with rational numbers, and A.rref().numerical_approx(digits=4) shows a decimal approximation. From the reduced row echelon form of an augmented matrix we describe the solution space of the linear system.

concepts.name: Rows and columns of a matrix
concepts.statement: A matrix has a certain number of rows and columns: a matrix with three rows and five columns is a 3 × 5 matrix, and a matrix with the same number of rows as columns, n, is an n × n matrix.

concepts.name: Augmentation of a matrix
concepts.statement: We say that a matrix B is an augmentation of a matrix A when it is obtained from A by adding some more columns; an augmented matrix is an augmentation of its coefficient matrix.

concepts.name: Augmentation Principle
concepts.statement: If matrix B is an augmentation of matrix A, then the reduced row echelon form of B is an augmentation of the reduced row echelon form of A. In particular, the reduced row echelon form of a coefficient matrix is found by looking inside the reduced row echelon form of the augmented matrix.

concepts.name: Computational effort of row reduction
concepts.statement: Measuring effort by the number of multiplications and additions, scaling a row of an n × n matrix requires n operations, an interchange none, and a replacement 2n. Roughly n² replacements and n scalings are needed to reach the reduced row echelon form, about 2n³ + n² operations in all, so the number of operations required to find the reduced row echelon form of an n × n matrix is roughly proportional to n³; a more careful accounting gives ⅔n³. If the size of the matrix grows by a factor of 10, the effort grows by a factor of 1000; a trillion equations in a trillion unknowns would take about 10¹⁶ years at a trillion operations a second.

concepts.name: Pivot position
concepts.statement: A pivot position in a matrix A is the position of a leading entry in the reduced row echelon matrix of A. We refer to pivot positions by their row and column number, saying, for instance, that there is a pivot position in the third row and fourth column.

concepts.name: Pivots per row and column
concepts.statement: A row contains at most one pivot position and a column contains at most one, so a 3 × 5 matrix has at most three pivot positions and so does a 5 × 3 matrix. A matrix with a pivot position in every row and every column must necessarily have the same number of rows and columns.

concepts.name: Two Fundamental Questions
concepts.statement: When we encounter a linear system, we often ask two questions. Existence: is there a solution to the linear system? Uniqueness: if the linear system is consistent, is the solution unique or are there infinitely many solutions? These two questions represent two sides of a coin that appear in many variations throughout our explorations; the location of the pivots influences the answers to both.

concepts.name: Consistent system
concepts.statement: If there is a solution to a linear system, we say that the system is consistent.

concepts.name: Inconsistent system
concepts.statement: If there is no solution to a linear system, we say it is inconsistent.

concepts.name: Inconsistency and a pivot in the rightmost column
concepts.statement: A linear system is inconsistent if and only if there is a pivot position in the rightmost column of the corresponding augmented matrix. Such a row says 0x + 0y + 0z = 1, which cannot be satisfied for any (x, y, z), while a row whose entries are all zero says 0 = 0 and has no effect on the solution space.

concepts.name: A pivot in every row gives a consistent system
concepts.statement: If every row of the coefficient matrix has a pivot position, then the corresponding system of linear equations is consistent: by the Augmentation Principle the reduced row echelon form of the coefficient matrix sits inside that of the augmented matrix, so there is no way to obtain a pivot in the rightmost column of the augmented matrix.

concepts.name: Pivots and the uniqueness of solutions
concepts.statement: Suppose that we consider a consistent linear system. If every column of the coefficient matrix contains a pivot position, then the system has a unique solution. If there is a column in the coefficient matrix that contains no pivot position, then the system has infinitely many solutions. Columns that contain a pivot position correspond to basic variables while columns that do not correspond to free variables; we adopt the convention that free variables correspond to columns without a pivot position.

concepts.name: Equations needed for a unique solution
concepts.statement: When a linear system has a unique solution, every column of the coefficient matrix has a pivot position; since every row contains at most one pivot position, there must be at least as many rows as columns, so the linear system has at least as many equations as variables. A consistent system with more variables than equations must have a free variable and so infinitely many solutions.

concepts.name: Reading existence and uniqueness from the pivots
concepts.statement: Determining whether a linear system is consistent, and whether its solution is unique, from the pivot positions of its reduced row echelon augmented matrix: a pivot in the rightmost column means the system is inconsistent; otherwise a pivot in every column of the coefficient matrix means a unique solution and a column without one means infinitely many, the pivot columns naming the basic variables and the others the free variables, from which a parametric description is written.

concepts.name: Vector
concepts.statement: A vector is most simply thought of as a matrix with a single column, such as v = [2, 1] or w = [−3, 1, 0, 2]. The entries in a vector are called its components; since v has two components, it is a two-dimensional vector, and w is a four-dimensional vector. A two-dimensional vector can be drawn as an arrow describing a walk in the plane, two units horizontally and one unit vertically for v, most frequently begun at the origin.

concepts.name: Space of m-dimensional vectors
concepts.statement: We denote the set of all m-dimensional vectors by ℝᵐ. Consequently, if u is a 3-dimensional vector, we say that u is in ℝ³.

concepts.name: Scalar
concepts.statement: We will frequently refer to real numbers, such as −3 in the scalar multiple −3v, as scalars to distinguish them from vectors.

concepts.name: Scalar multiplication
concepts.statement: We multiply a vector v by a real number c by multiplying each of the components of v by c; for instance, −3[2, −4, 1] = [−6, 12, −3].

concepts.name: Vector addition
concepts.statement: We add two vectors of the same dimension by adding their components; for instance, [2, −4, 3] + [−5, 6, −3] = [−3, 2, 0].

concepts.name: Geometry of scalar multiplication and vector addition
concepts.statement: Scalar multiplication has the effect of stretching or compressing a vector, and multiplying by a negative scalar changes its direction; in either case a scalar multiple of v lies on the same line defined by v. To represent the sum v + w, we walk from the origin with the horizontal and vertical changes given by v and continue with those prescribed by w, placing the tail of w on the tip of v; alternatively, the sum is the diagonal of the parallelogram with v and w as two sides.

concepts.name: Vectors and points interchangeably
concepts.statement: At times it is useful to think of vectors and points interchangeably: the vector [2, 1] describes the point (2, 1) and vice-versa. When we say that the vectors of the form cv + w form a line, we really mean that the tips of the vectors all lie on the line passing through w and parallel to v.

concepts.name: Line described by vectors
concepts.statement: The set of vectors having the form cv is a line. To form the set of vectors cv + w, we begin with the vector w and add multiples of v, moving from the tip of w in a direction parallel to v; the effect is to translate the line cv by the vector w, so the set of vectors cv + w forms a line through w parallel to v.

concepts.name: Properties of vector operations
concepts.statement: Even though these vector operations are new, it is straightforward to check that some familiar properties hold: commutativity, v + w = w + v, and distributivity, a(v + w) = av + aw.

concepts.name: Working with vectors in Sage
concepts.statement: Defining a vector in Sage with the vector command, such as v = vector([3,1]), and performing scalar multiplication and vector addition with * and +, as in print(2*v) and print(v + w).

concepts.name: Linear combination
concepts.statement: The linear combination of the vectors v₁, v₂, …, vₙ with scalars c₁, c₂, …, cₙ is the vector c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + … + cₙvₙ. The scalars c₁, c₂, …, cₙ are called the weights of the linear combination. Geometrically, cv + dw is found by walking along v a total of c times followed by walking along w a total of d times; when one weight is held constant while the other varies, the vector moves along a line.

concepts.name: Linear combinations and linear systems
concepts.statement: The vector b is a linear combination of the vectors v₁, v₂, …, vₙ if and only if the linear system corresponding to the augmented matrix [v₁ v₂ … vₙ | b] is consistent. A solution to this linear system gives weights c₁, c₂, …, cₙ such that c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + … + cₙvₙ = b. Asking whether b is a linear combination of v₁, …, vₙ is therefore equivalent to asking whether an associated linear system is consistent.

concepts.name: Writing a vector as a linear combination
concepts.statement: Deciding whether b is a linear combination of v₁, v₂, …, vₙ, and finding the weights: write the equation c₁v₁ + … + cₙvₙ = b component by component as a linear system, construct its augmented matrix [v₁ v₂ … vₙ | b], and find the reduced row echelon form. The weights are read from the solution; they are the only possible weights when there is a pivot position in every column, there are infinitely many choices when a column lacks one, and there are none when the system is inconsistent. When the coefficient matrix [v₁ v₂ … vₙ] has a pivot position in every row, every vector b is a linear combination; when some row lacks a pivot, as for two vectors on the same line, a pivot can appear in the rightmost column of the augmented matrix for some choice of b.

concepts.name: Columns of a matrix as vectors
concepts.statement: We may think of the columns of a matrix as a set of vectors: a 3 × 4 matrix may be represented as [v₁ v₂ v₃ v₄] where v₁, …, v₄ are its columns, so the 3 × 4 matrix is equivalent to an ordered set of 4 vectors in ℝ³. If we say that the shape of a matrix is m × n, we mean that it has m rows and n columns.

concepts.name: Scalar multiplication of a matrix
concepts.statement: We define scalar multiplication of a matrix using the column-wise vector operation: c[v₁ v₂ … vₙ] = [cv₁ cv₂ … cvₙ], a natural extension of its vector counterpart.

concepts.name: Matrix addition
concepts.statement: We define matrix addition using the column-wise vector operation: [v₁ v₂ … vₙ] + [w₁ w₂ … wₙ] = [v₁ + w₁ v₂ + w₂ … vₙ + wₙ]. Some care is required: since we need the same number of vectors to add and those vectors must be of the same dimension, two matrices must have the same shape if we wish to form their sum.

concepts.name: Identity matrix
concepts.statement: The matrix Iₙ, which we call the identity matrix, is the n × n matrix whose entries are zero except for the diagonal entries, all of which are 1; for instance, I₃ has rows [1 0 0], [0 1 0], [0 0 1]. The sum A + Iₙ can be formed only when A is n × n. Multiplying a vector by I produces the same vector, Ix = x, which is why I is called the identity matrix.

concepts.name: Matrix-vector multiplication
concepts.statement: The product of a matrix A by a vector x is the linear combination of the columns of A using the components of x as weights: if A = [v₁ v₂ … vₙ] and x has components c₁, c₂, …, cₙ, then Ax = c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + … + cₙvₙ. If A is an m × n matrix, then x must be an n-dimensional vector, and the product Ax will be an m-dimensional vector.

forms.condition: A = [v₁ v₂ … vₙ], x the vector of weights c₁, …, cₙ

concepts.name: Row shortcut for a matrix-vector product
concepts.statement: There is a shortcut for computing the product Ax. To find the first component of the product, we consider the first row of the matrix, multiply the first entry in that row by the first component of the vector, the second entry by the second component, and so on, and add the results; the third component comes in the same way from the third row, as 2(3) + 3(1) = 9 in the example.

concepts.name: Zero vector
concepts.statement: A vector whose entries are all zero is denoted by 0. For any matrix A, the product A0 = 0.

concepts.name: Multiplying matrices and vectors in Sage
concepts.statement: Finding the product of a matrix and a vector, or of two matrices, in Sage with the * operator, after defining them with matrix(2,2,[1,2,2,1]) and vector([3,-1]): A*v and A*B.

concepts.name: Linearity of matrix multiplication
concepts.statement: If A is a matrix, v and w vectors of the appropriate dimensions, and c a scalar, then A0 = 0, A(cv) = cAv, and A(v + w) = Av + Aw.

concepts.name: Matrix equation
concepts.statement: Beginning with a matrix A and a vector b, we ask whether we can find a vector x such that Ax = b. The equation Ax = b gives a notationally compact way to write a linear system: writing A = [v₁ v₂ … vₙ], we frequently write the augmented matrix [v₁ v₂ … vₙ | b] = [A | b] and say that the matrix A is augmented by the vector b.

concepts.name: Three views of a matrix equation
concepts.statement: If A = [v₁ v₂ … vₙ] and x has components x₁, x₂, …, xₙ, then the following statements are equivalent: the vector x satisfies the equation Ax = b; the vector b is a linear combination of the columns of A with weights xⱼ, x₁v₁ + x₂v₂ + … + xₙvₙ = b; and the components of x form a solution to the linear system corresponding to the augmented matrix [v₁ v₂ … vₙ | b]. These are three different ways of looking at the same solution space.

concepts.name: Solution space written in vector form
concepts.statement: Since we asked to describe the solutions to Ax = b, we express the parametric description in terms of the vector x: with x₃ free, x = [−x₃, 5 + 2x₃, x₃] = [0, 5, 0] + x₃[−1, 2, 1], so the solutions may be written in the form v + x₃w for appropriate vectors v and w. Geometrically, the solution space is a line in ℝ³ through v moving parallel to w.

concepts.name: Matrix-matrix multiplication
concepts.statement: Given matrices A and B, we form their product AB by first writing B in terms of its columns, B = [v₁ v₂ … vₚ], and then defining AB = [Av₁ Av₂ … Avₚ].

concepts.name: Shape of a matrix product
concepts.statement: We can only multiply matrices if their shapes are compatible: when constructing AB, the matrix A multiplies the columns of B, so the number of columns of A must equal the number of rows of B. When this condition is met, the number of rows of AB is the number of rows of A and the number of columns of AB is the number of columns of B; if A is m × n and B is n × p, then AB is m × p.

concepts.name: Properties of matrix-matrix multiplication
concepts.statement: If A, B, and C are matrices such that the following operations are defined, it follows that multiplication is associative, A(BC) = (AB)C, and distributive, A(B + C) = AB + AC and (A + B)C = AC + BC.

concepts.name: Properties of real numbers that fail for matrices
concepts.statement: A few properties that hold for real numbers do not hold for matrices. Commutativity: it is not generally true that AB = BA. Cancellation: it is not generally true that AB = AC implies that B = C. Zero divisors: it is not generally true that AB = 0 implies that either A = 0 or B = 0.

concepts.name: Span
concepts.statement: The span of a set of vectors v₁, v₂, …, vₙ is the set of all linear combinations that can be formed from the vectors. Alternatively, if A = [v₁ v₂ … vₙ], then the span of the vectors consists of all vectors b for which the equation Ax = b is consistent.

concepts.name: Notation for the span
concepts.statement: We will denote the span of the set of vectors v₁, v₂, …, vₙ by Span{v₁, v₂, …, vₙ}. Because span is a concept that is connected to a set of vectors, we say “The span of the set of vectors v₁, v₂, …, vₙ is …”; rather than “The span of the matrix A is …,” we say “The span of the columns of the matrix A is ….”

concepts.name: Span as the points reached by walking
concepts.statement: We can think of a linear combination of two vectors v and w as a recipe for walking in the plane: we first move a prescribed amount in the direction of v and then a prescribed amount in the direction of w. The span consists of all the places we can walk to. For v = [2, 0] and w = [−1, 1] we can walk to any point in the plane, so Span{v, w} = ℝ²; for w = −2v every linear combination cv + dw = (c − 2d)v is a scalar multiple of v, so the span is the line defined by v and we can only walk to points on this line.

concepts.name: Deciding whether a vector is in a span
concepts.statement: To determine whether b is in the span of v₁, …, vₙ, we form the matrix A = [v₁ v₂ … vₙ] and consider the equation Ax = b: reducing the augmented matrix [A | b] shows the system consistent, and b in the span, or inconsistent, and b not in it. When the coefficient matrix has a pivot position in every row, the augmented matrix cannot have a pivot in its rightmost column, so every vector is in the span.

concepts.name: Spans of vectors in three dimensions
concepts.statement: The types of sets that appear as the span of a set of vectors in ℝ³ are relatively simple. With a single nonzero vector, all linear combinations are scalar multiples of that vector, so the span is a line; the matrix formed by this vector has one pivot position. The span of two vectors that do not lie on the same line is a plane, and their matrix has two pivot positions. A set of three vectors whose matrix has three pivot positions, one in every row, has span ℝ³, since no augmentation of that matrix can have a pivot in the rightmost column. With one, two, or three pivot positions, the span is a line, a plane, or ℝ³.

concepts.name: Pivot positions and span
concepts.statement: Suppose we have vectors v₁, v₂, …, vₙ in ℝᵐ. Then Span{v₁, v₂, …, vₙ} = ℝᵐ if and only if the matrix [v₁ v₂ … vₙ] has a pivot position in every row.

forms.condition: the matrix [v₁ v₂ … vₙ] has a pivot position in every row

concepts.name: Vectors needed to span a space
concepts.statement: A set of vectors whose span is ℝᵐ contains at least m vectors. If n vectors span ℝᵐ, their matrix has a pivot position in every row, and since a matrix can have at most one pivot position in a column, there must be at least as many columns as rows, n ≥ m; a set of vectors that spans ℝ⁶³² has at least 632 vectors. Intuitively, we need at least m directions to have the flexibility needed to reach every point in ℝᵐ.

concepts.name: Describing a span geometrically
concepts.statement: Giving a geometric description of the span of a set of vectors from the pivot positions of their matrix: in ℝ³ a span with one, two, or three pivot positions is a line, a plane, or ℝ³, and in ℝᵐ the columns span ℝᵐ exactly when every row has a pivot position; and constructing matrices whose columns span a given line, plane, or space.

concepts.name: Linear independence
concepts.statement: A set of vectors is called linearly dependent if one of the vectors is a linear combination of the others. Otherwise, the set of vectors is called linearly independent. For the sake of completeness, we say that a set of vectors containing only one nonzero vector is linearly independent.

concepts.name: A dependent vector adds nothing to the span
concepts.statement: When w₃ = −2w₁ − w₂, any linear combination c₁w₁ + c₂w₂ + c₃w₃ = (c₁ − 2c₃)w₁ + (c₂ − c₃)w₂ may be written using only w₁ and w₂, so Span{w₁, w₂, w₃} = Span{w₁, w₂}: adding the vector w₃ does not change the span. Geometrically, a third vector that is a linear combination of two others already lies in the plane they form, so the span remains a plane, while a vector that is not a linear combination of the others provides an independent direction to move and the span of the three vectors is ℝ³.

forms.condition: w₃ a linear combination of w₁ and w₂

concepts.name: Pivot positions and linear independence
concepts.statement: The columns of a matrix are linearly independent if and only if every column contains a pivot position. A vector corresponding to a column without a pivot position can be expressed as a linear combination of the vectors whose columns do contain pivot positions, as viewing the first three columns as an augmented matrix shows; when every column has a pivot, viewing the columns as an augmented matrix gives an inconsistent system, so none of the vectors is a linear combination of the others.

concepts.name: Size of a linearly independent set
concepts.statement: A linearly independent set of vectors in ℝᵐ contains at most m vectors: the associated matrix must have a pivot position in every column, and since every row contains at most one pivot position, the number of columns can be no greater than the number of rows. Any linearly independent set in ℝ³ can contain no more than three vectors, the three independent directions up/down, front/back, left/right of our three-dimensional world.

concepts.name: Homogeneous equation
concepts.statement: If A is a matrix, we call the equation Ax = 0 a homogeneous equation. It always has at least one solution, the vector x = 0; any other solution is a nonzero solution. The uniqueness of solutions to this equation reflects on the linear independence of the columns of A.

concepts.name: Equivalent conditions for linear dependence
concepts.statement: For a matrix A = [v₁ v₂ … vₙ], the following statements are equivalent: the columns of A are linearly dependent; one of the vectors v₁, v₂, …, vₙ is a linear combination of the others; the matrix A has a column without a pivot position; the homogeneous equation Ax = 0 has infinitely many solutions and hence a nonzero solution; there are weights c₁, c₂, …, cₙ, not all of which are zero, such that c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + … + cₙvₙ = 0.

concepts.name: Testing a set of vectors for linear independence
concepts.statement: Deciding whether vectors are linearly dependent or independent by viewing them as the columns of a matrix and finding its reduced row echelon form: a pivot position in every column means independence; a column without one means dependence, and a nonzero solution of the homogeneous equation Ax = 0, read from the free variable, gives weights with c₁v₁ + … + cₙvₙ = 0, which can be rearranged to write one vector as a linear combination of the others.

concepts.name: Span and linear independence compared
concepts.statement: Span addresses the existence of solutions and linear independence their uniqueness, and the results of the two sections run in parallel. A vector b is in the span of a set of vectors if it is a linear combination of them, while a set is linearly dependent if one vector is a linear combination of the others; b is in Span{v₁, …, vₙ} if there exists a solution to Ax = b, while v₁, …, vₙ are linearly independent if x = 0 is the unique solution to Ax = 0; the columns of an m × n matrix span ℝᵐ if the matrix has a pivot position in every row, while they are linearly independent if it has a pivot position in every column; a set that spans ℝᵐ has at least m vectors, while a linearly independent set in ℝᵐ has at most m.

concepts.name: Matrix transformation
concepts.statement: The matrix transformation associated to the matrix A is the function that assigns to the vector x the vector Ax; that is, T(x) = Ax. If A is an m × n matrix, x needs to be an n-dimensional vector and the product Ax will be m-dimensional, so we write T: ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ to indicate that T takes vectors in ℝⁿ as inputs and produces vectors in ℝᵐ as outputs.

concepts.name: Standard basis vectors
concepts.statement: We write the columns of the n × n identity matrix as e₁ = [1, 0, …, 0], e₂ = [0, 1, …, 0], …, eₙ = [0, 0, …, 1], each with a single entry 1 and zeros elsewhere, so that any vector x = x₁e₁ + x₂e₂ + … + xₙeₙ.

concepts.name: Matrix of a matrix transformation
concepts.statement: If T: ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ is a matrix transformation given by T(x) = Ax, then the matrix A has columns T(eⱼ); that is, A = [T(e₁) T(e₂) … T(eₙ)]. Since T(eⱼ) = [v₁ v₂ … vₙ]eⱼ = vⱼ, the jth column of A is found by evaluating T(eⱼ), so we can reconstruct A from some output values of T.

concepts.name: Finding the matrix of a matrix transformation
concepts.statement: Identifying the matrix A of a matrix transformation T: from a formula for T(x) in terms of the components of x, by rewriting the output as x₁ times a column plus x₂ times a column and so on; or from the outputs T(e₁), T(e₂), …, which are the columns of A, as for a 90° rotation or a bakery whose hourly production gives each column. Reading the shape of A from T: ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ, where A is m × n.

concepts.name: Composition of matrix transformations
concepts.statement: If T: ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ and S: ℝᵐ → ℝᵖ are matrix transformations with associated matrices A and B respectively, then the composition S ∘ T, obtained by first performing T and then S, is also a matrix transformation whose associated matrix is the product BA: (S ∘ T)(x) = S(T(x)) = S(Ax) = BAx = (BA)x. The transformations must be compatible: the inputs to S must be m-dimensional, the same condition needed to form the product BA.

concepts.name: State vector
concepts.statement: We have a vector x that describes the state of some system; in the example, x describes the distribution of trucks between the two locations at a particular time. We call x the state vector.

concepts.name: Transition function
concepts.statement: There is a matrix transformation T(x) = Ax that describes the state at some later time. We call T the transition function, as it describes the transition of the state vector from one time to the next.

concepts.name: Discrete dynamical system
concepts.statement: Beginning with an initial state x₀, the state evolves over time: x₁ = T(x₀) = Ax₀, x₂ = T(x₁) = (T ∘ T)(x₀) = A²x₀, x₃ = T(x₂) = A³x₀, and so on. We call this situation, where the state of a system evolves from one time to the next according to the rule xₖ₊₁ = Axₖ, a discrete dynamical system. Powers of the matrix A determine the long-term behavior of the state vector.

concepts.name: Geometric operations as matrix transformations
concepts.statement: Matrix transformations provide a convenient way to describe geometric operations. Reflection across the horizontal axis takes [x, y] to [x, −y], with matrix [1 0; 0 −1]; [2 0; 0 1] stretches by a factor of 2 in the horizontal direction and [2 0; 0 2] uniformly in all directions; [0 1; −1 0] is a 90° clockwise rotation and [0 −1; 1 0] a 90° counterclockwise rotation; [1 1; 0 1] is a shear, which pushes vectors horizontally an amount equal to the vertical component; [−1 0; 0 1] reflects vectors in the vertical axis and [0 1; 1 0] across the line y = x; [1 0; 0 0] is a projection, which produces the shadow of the vector on the horizontal axis; [1 0; 0 1] is the identity, which causes no change; and [1 −1; −2 2] pushes vectors onto the line defined by [1, −2]. The matrix of each is found from the columns T(e₁) and T(e₂).

forms.condition: stretch by a factor of 2 in the horizontal direction
stretch by a factor of 2 uniformly in all directions
reflection across the line y = x

concepts.name: Rotation matrix
concepts.statement: The matrix that rotates vectors counterclockwise by an angle θ is [cos θ −sin θ; sin θ cos θ], since rotating the vector [1, 0] by θ gives [cos θ, sin θ]. For the rotation by 45°, T(e₁) has length 1 and is the hypotenuse of a right isosceles triangle, so by Pythagoras' theorem its legs are 1/√2, T(e₁) = [1/√2, 1/√2], T(e₂) = [−1/√2, 1/√2], and A = [1/√2 −1/√2; 1/√2 1/√2].

concepts.name: Linearity of matrix transformations
concepts.statement: The function T: ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ is a matrix transformation, T(x) = Ax for some m × n matrix A, if and only if T(cv) = cT(v) and T(v + w) = T(v) + T(w). A matrix transformation satisfies these linearity properties because A(cv) = cAv and A(v + w) = Av + Aw; conversely, if T satisfies them, then A = [T(e₁) T(e₂) … T(eₙ)] works, since T(x) = T(x₁e₁ + … + xₙeₙ) = x₁T(e₁) + … + xₙT(eₙ) = x₁Ae₁ + … + xₙAeₙ = A(x₁e₁ + … + xₙeₙ) = Ax. If we can verify the two linearity properties for a function, as for a rotation, where scaling then rotating is the same as rotating then scaling and a rotation carries the parallelogram of v and w to that of T(v) and T(w), then we know that it is a matrix transformation.

concepts.name: Composing geometric transformations
concepts.statement: Finding the transformation that results from performing one geometric operation and then another by multiplying their matrices, read right to left: reflecting across the line y = x twice gives the identity, rotating by 90° then reflecting in y = x gives [1 0; 0 −1], reflecting then rotating gives [−1 0; 0 1], composing a 90° rotation with itself four times gives the identity, and a composition of two reflections is a rotation through twice the angle between their lines. The order matters, since matrix multiplication is not commutative.

concepts.name: Matrix transformations in computer animation
concepts.statement: Linear algebra plays a significant role in computer animation. Animators define a character and create the illusion of motion by drawing it in a sequence of frames in which the character's pose is modified slightly from one frame to the next, often using matrix transformations: a two-dimensional character is reflected to wave with the other hand, rotated by 45° at a time through a cartwheel, zoomed by translating and then scaling, and given a shadow by a shear followed by a vertical compression, each pose a composition of matrix transformations.

concepts.name: Translation
concepts.statement: Motions that simply move a character to a different position in the plane are called translations. This presents a problem because a matrix transformation T: ℝ² → ℝ² has the property that T(0) = A0 = 0, which means that a matrix transformation cannot move the origin of the coordinate plane.

concepts.name: Homogeneous coordinates
concepts.statement: To translate a character, animators use homogeneous coordinates, formed by placing the two-dimensional coordinate plane inside ℝ³ as the plane z = 1: rather than describing points in the plane as vectors [x, y], we describe them as three-dimensional vectors [x, y, 1]. A matrix of the form [a b c; d e f; 0 0 1] transforms points in the plane z = 1 into points in the same plane, x′ = ax + by + c and y′ = dx + ey + f, and the entries c and f are responsible for the translation: [1 0 2; 0 1 1; 0 0 1] moves the character two units horizontally and one unit vertically.

concepts.name: Square matrix
concepts.statement: We only define invertibility for matrices that have the same number of rows and columns, in which case we say that the matrix is square.

concepts.name: Invertible matrix
concepts.statement: An n × n matrix A is called invertible if there is a matrix B such that AB = I_n, where I_n is the n × n identity matrix. Just as the real number 0 has no multiplicative inverse, we should not expect every matrix to have one; the matrix [−2 1; 4 −2], for instance, is not invertible, since the equation for the first column of its inverse is inconsistent.

concepts.name: Inverse of a matrix
concepts.statement: If A is invertible, the matrix B with AB = I_n is called the inverse of A and denoted A⁻¹. It plays the role that the multiplicative inverse 3⁻¹ = 1/3 plays for the number 3 in the equation 3x = 5.

concepts.name: Solving an equation with the inverse
concepts.statement: If A is an invertible matrix with inverse B, then any equation Ax = b is consistent and x = Bb is a solution, since A(Bb) = (AB)b = Ib = b. In other words, the solution to Ax = b is x = A⁻¹b, just as the solution to 3x = 5 is x = (1/3)·5; it is the solution, since A has a pivot position in every column.

concepts.name: Invertibility and the reduced row echelon form
concepts.statement: The matrix A is invertible if and only if the reduced row echelon form of A is the identity matrix: A ∼ I. Since Ax = b is consistent for every vector b, the columns of A must span ℝⁿ, so there is a pivot position in every row; since A is also square, there is a pivot position in every column, and its reduced row echelon form is the identity.

concepts.name: Finding an inverse by row reduction
concepts.statement: To find the inverse B = [b₁ b₂] of a 2 × 2 matrix A we require AB = [Ab₁ Ab₂] = I, so the columns of B solve Ab₁ = [1, 0] and Ab₂ = [0, 1]. Rather than solving these equations separately, we augment A by both vectors, that is, by the identity, and find the reduced row echelon form: [A | I] ∼ [I | A⁻¹]. This reformulation always works for an invertible n × n matrix.

forms.condition: B = [b₁ b₂] the inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix A

concepts.name: The inverse of an inverse
concepts.statement: The product of two matrices depends on the order in which they are multiplied, but something fortunate happens for invertibility: if A is an n × n matrix and AB = I, then it is also true that BA = I, which tells us that B is invertible with inverse A. In other words, (A⁻¹)⁻¹ = A, and A and B are inverses of each other. Exercise 3.1.12 explains why it always happens.

concepts.name: The inverse of a product
concepts.statement: If A and B are two invertible n × n matrices, then their product AB is also invertible and (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹, since (AB)(B⁻¹A⁻¹) = A(BB⁻¹)A⁻¹ = AIA⁻¹ = AA⁻¹ = I by associativity.

concepts.name: Properties of invertible matrices
concepts.statement: An n × n matrix A is invertible if and only if A ∼ I. If A is invertible, then the solution to the equation Ax = b is given by x = A⁻¹b. We can find A⁻¹ by finding the reduced row echelon form of [A | I]; namely, [A | I] ∼ [I | A⁻¹]. If A and B are two invertible n × n matrices, then their product AB is also invertible and (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.

concepts.name: Inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix
concepts.statement: There is a simple formula for finding the inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix: [a b; c d]⁻¹ = (1/(ad − bc))[d −b; −c a], which can be easily checked. The condition that A be invertible is, in this case, reduced to the condition that ad − bc ≠ 0, a condition understood better through determinants. There is a similar formula for a 3 × 3 matrix, but there is not a good reason to write it.

forms.latex: \left[\begin{array}{rr} a & b \\ c & d \end{array}\right]^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad-bc} \left[\begin{array}{rr} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{array}\right]

concepts.name: Triangular matrix
concepts.statement: We say that a matrix A is lower triangular if all its entries above the diagonal are zero. Similarly, A is upper triangular if all the entries below the diagonal are zero.

concepts.name: Invertibility of a triangular matrix
concepts.statement: An n × n triangular matrix is invertible if and only if the entries on the diagonal are all nonzero. When the diagonal entries are nonzero, Gaussian elimination finds a pivot position in every row; a zero on the diagonal leads to a row without a pivot position.

concepts.name: Elementary matrix
concepts.statement: An elementary matrix performs a row operation on a matrix by multiplication: it is constructed by applying the desired operation to the identity matrix. For a matrix having three rows, multiplying the second row by 3 and adding it to the third is performed by L = [1 0 0; 0 1 0; 0 3 1] (we often use L because these matrices are lower triangular), multiplying the third row by 2 by S = [1 0 0; 0 1 0; 0 0 2], and interchanging the first two rows by P = [0 1 0; 1 0 0; 0 0 1].

forms.condition: multiplying the second row by 3 and adding it to the third

concepts.name: Permutation matrix
concepts.statement: A matrix P that interchanges two rows of a matrix, obtained by interchanging those rows of the identity matrix, is usually called a permutation matrix. It is its own inverse, P = P⁻¹, because we can undo the interchange operation by repeating it.

concepts.name: Row operations as matrix multiplication
concepts.statement: The row operations of replacement, scaling and interchange can be performed by multiplying by elementary matrices: if R is obtained by applying an operation to the identity, then RA is the result of applying that operation to A. Each elementary matrix is invertible, its inverse performing the operation that undoes it: a replacement that adds −2 times the first row to the second is undone by adding 2 times the first row, a scaling by 4 by a scaling by 1/4, and an interchange by itself. The forward substitution phase of Gaussian elimination is a product of such matrices, L₃L₂L₁A = U.

concepts.name: LU factorization
concepts.statement: Since L₃L₂L₁A = U, we have A = (L₃L₂L₁)⁻¹U = LU, where L = (L₃L₂L₁)⁻¹ = L₁⁻¹L₂⁻¹L₃⁻¹ is lower triangular. This way of writing A = LU as the product of a lower and an upper triangular matrix is known as an LU factorization of A; its usefulness is explored in Section 5.1.

concepts.name: Basis
concepts.statement: A set of vectors v₁, v₂, …, vₙ in ℝᵐ is called a basis for ℝᵐ if the set of vectors spans ℝᵐ and is linearly independent. Rather than continuing to write a list of vectors, we denote a basis using a single symbol, such as 𝓑 = {v₁, v₂, …, vₘ}.

concepts.name: Testing a set of vectors for a basis
concepts.statement: A set of vectors forms a basis for ℝᵐ if and only if the matrix A = [v₁ v₂ ⋯ vₙ] ∼ I. The span of the vectors is ℝᵐ if and only if A has a pivot position in every row, and the vectors are linearly independent if and only if A has a pivot position in every column, so a basis requires a pivot in every row and every column.

forms.condition: v₁, v₂, …, vₙ a basis for ℝᵐ

concepts.name: Number of vectors in a basis
concepts.statement: Since the matrix A = [v₁ v₂ ⋯ vₙ] has a pivot position in every row and every column, it must have the same number of rows as columns. Therefore, the number of vectors in a basis for ℝᵐ must be m: a basis for ℝ²³ must have exactly 23 vectors.

concepts.name: Standard basis
concepts.statement: The vectors e₁, e₂, e₃ form the columns of the 3 × 3 identity matrix, which implies that this set forms a basis for ℝ³. More generally, the set of vectors e₁, e₂, …, eₘ forms a basis for ℝᵐ, which we call the standard basis for ℝᵐ; in the standard basis 𝓔, the coordinates of a vector are the vector itself.

concepts.name: Coordinate system defined by a basis
concepts.statement: A basis for ℝᵐ forms a coordinate system for ℝᵐ. In the standard coordinate system, the point (2, −3) is found by moving 2 units to the right and 3 units down; in the coordinate system defined by the basis 𝓑 = {v₁, v₂}, we interpret (2, −3) to mean we move two times along v₁ and 3 times along −v₂, which leaves us at the point (1, −4) in the usual coordinates. The grid of streets in a city gives a more natural coordinate system than north-south, east-west coordinates in the same way.

concepts.name: Unique representation in a basis
concepts.statement: Suppose that 𝓑 = {v₁, v₂, …, vₘ} is a basis for ℝᵐ. The span of the vectors is ℝᵐ, which implies that any vector x in ℝᵐ can be written as a linear combination of the vectors; the vectors are linearly independent, which means that we can write x as a linear combination in exactly one way. Therefore x = c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + … + cₘvₘ where the weights c₁, c₂, …, cₘ are unique.

concepts.name: Coordinates of a vector in a basis
concepts.statement: The coordinates of the vector x in the coordinate system defined by the basis 𝓑 are the weights that we use to create x as a linear combination of the basis vectors: {x}_𝓑 denotes the vector [c₁, c₂, …, cₘ] of weights such that x = c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + … + cₘvₘ. For instance, since [1, −4] = 2v₁ − 3v₂ for v₁ = [2, 1], v₂ = [1, 2], we write {[1, −4]}_𝓑 = [2, −3].

concepts.name: Finding the coordinates of a vector in a basis
concepts.statement: Knowing the coordinates {x}_𝓑 = [c₁, c₂], we find x as the linear combination c₁v₁ + c₂v₂. Knowing x in standard coordinates, we find its coordinates in the basis 𝓑 by solving the linear system c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ = x, whose augmented matrix [v₁ v₂ | x] we row reduce: for x = [−8, 2] and the basis v₁ = [2, 1], v₂ = [1, 2], [2 1 | −8; 1 2 | 2] ∼ [1 0 | −6; 0 1 | 4], so {x}_𝓑 = [−6, 4].

concepts.name: Change-of-basis matrix
concepts.statement: We use P_𝓑 to denote the matrix whose columns are the basis vectors, P_𝓑 = [v₁ v₂ ⋯ vₘ]. Since x = c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + … + cₘvₘ = [v₁ v₂ ⋯ vₘ]{x}_𝓑, the matrix P_𝓑 converts coordinates in the basis 𝓑 into standard coordinates. Since its columns are the basis vectors, P_𝓑 ∼ I_m, and P_𝓑 is therefore invertible.

concepts.name: Converting between coordinate systems
concepts.statement: If 𝓑 is a basis and P_𝓑 the matrix whose columns are the basis vectors, then x = P_𝓑{x}_𝓑 and {x}_𝓑 = P_𝓑⁻¹x. If we have another basis 𝓒, then x = P_𝓒{x}_𝓒 as well, so {x}_𝓑 = P_𝓑⁻¹x = P_𝓑⁻¹(P_𝓒{x}_𝓒) = (P_𝓑⁻¹P_𝓒){x}_𝓒: the matrix P_𝓑⁻¹P_𝓒 converts 𝓒-coordinates into 𝓑-coordinates.

concepts.name: Haar wavelet basis
concepts.statement: The basis 𝓑 of ℝ⁴ with v₁ = [1, 1, 1, 1], v₂ = [1, 1, −1, −1], v₃ = [1, −1, 0, 0], v₄ = [0, 0, 1, −1] is sometimes called a Haar wavelet basis, and the change of basis is known as a Haar wavelet transform. For a vector of quarterly revenue, the coefficient c₁ measures the average revenue over the year, c₂ the deviation from the annual average in the first and second halves of the year, and c₃ and c₄ how the quarters differ from the average of their half; the coefficients provide a view of the revenue over different time scales, from an annual summary to a finer view of quarterly behavior. This basis provides a useful way to store digital images.

concepts.name: Color model
concepts.statement: A color is represented digitally by a vector in ℝ³. There are different ways in which we can represent colors, depending on whether a computer or a human will be processing the color; these representations are called color models, and the JPEG compression algorithm uses two of them.

concepts.name: RGB color model
concepts.statement: Digital displays create colors by blending together various amounts of red, green, and blue, so we can describe a color by putting its constituent amounts of red, green, and blue into a vector [R, G, B]. The quantities R, G, and B are each stored with one byte of information, so they are integers between 0 and 255. This is called the RGB color model; it is most relevant in digital applications.

concepts.name: YCbCr color model
concepts.statement: We define a basis 𝓑 = {v₁, v₂, v₃} of ℝ³ with v₁ = [1, 1, 1], v₂ = [0, −0.34413, 1.77200], v₃ = [1.40200, −0.71414, 0] to define a new coordinate system with coordinates Y, C_b and C_r: {[R, G, B]}_𝓑 = [Y, C_b, C_r]. The luminance Y varies from 0 to 255 while the chrominances vary between −127.5 and 127.5. This is known as the YC_bC_r color model; it was created from research into human vision and concentrates the most visually important data into a single coordinate, the luminance, to which our eyes are most sensitive, so that some of the chrominance data can be safely ignored.

concepts.name: Luminance
concepts.statement: The coordinate Y of a color in the YC_bC_r color model is called luminance. It is a weighted average of the R, G and B values that roughly represents the brightness of the color; an image rendered with only its luminance looks like a grayscale version of the original with all its visual detail, which is what a black-and-white television displayed.

concepts.name: Chrominance
concepts.statement: The coordinates C_b and C_r of a color in the YC_bC_r color model are called blue and red chrominance, respectively. The blue chrominance roughly measures the amount of blue in the color and the red chrominance the amount of red; an image rendered with only one chrominance carries considerably less visual detail than the luminance, so more of its data can be discarded.

concepts.name: Discrete Fourier Transform
concepts.statement: The JPEG compression algorithm uses the Discrete Fourier Transform, the change of basis defined by the basis 𝓑 = {v₀, v₁, …, v₇} of ℝ⁸ whose vector v_j has components cos((2i + 1)jπ/16) for i = 0, 1, …, 7. The basis vectors vary at different rates: v₀ is constantly 1, v₁ varies relatively slowly, v₂ a little more rapidly, and v₇ quite rapidly. In the resulting coordinate system the first coefficient is the average of the components of a vector, F₀ = (x₀ + x₁ + … + x₇)/8, and the other coefficients measure variations in the components away from the average.

concepts.name: Fourier coefficients
concepts.statement: Writing the vector x of luminance values in the coordinates of the Fourier basis, {x}_𝓑 = [F₀, F₁, …, F₇], the coordinates F_j are called the Fourier coefficients of the vector x. If the components of x vary relatively slowly, the coefficients F_j with larger values of j are small; for the first column of the block, F₀ = 151.6 is the largest and F₄ through F₇ are relatively small.

concepts.name: Approximating a vector from fewer Fourier coefficients
concepts.statement: To approximate a vector x, we round its Fourier coefficients to the nearest integer and set the coefficients of the rapidly varying basis vectors, or every coefficient whose absolute value is below a threshold, to zero; converting the approximate coefficients back into the standard coordinate system with P_𝓑 reconstructs a vector very close to the original. Setting F₆ and F₇ to zero changes the luminance values of the first column by at most one or two, a difference our eyes are not sensitive enough to detect.

concepts.name: JPEG compression algorithm
concepts.statement: The JPEG compression algorithm represents an image using a fraction of the data needed to display it by detecting redundancy with bases suited to the task. The image is broken into 8 × 8 blocks of pixels and the colors converted from the RGB to the YC_bC_r model. For each block, the Fourier coefficients of the columns of luminance values are formed and then the Fourier coefficients of the rows of that matrix; the result is rounded to integers, the coefficients whose absolute value falls below a threshold set by the quality parameter are set to zero, and only the nonzero coefficients are recorded, 12 of 64 at a high setting and 5 at a low one, with more of the chrominance coefficients discarded. The image is reconstructed by converting back; a lower quality setting saves more storage but reconstructs the image less accurately.

concepts.name: Area of a parallelogram
concepts.statement: The area of a parallelogram is found by multiplying the length of one side by the perpendicular distance to its parallel side: with base b and height h, the area is bh. Two parallelograms with the same base and the same height have the same area, even when one is sheared.

concepts.name: Orientation of a pair of vectors
concepts.statement: An ordered pair of vectors v₁ and v₂ is called positively oriented if the angle, measured in the counterclockwise direction, from v₁ to v₂ is less than 180°; we say the pair is negatively oriented if it is more than 180°.

concepts.name: Determinant
concepts.statement: Suppose a 2 × 2 matrix A has columns v₁ and v₂. If the pair of vectors is positively oriented, then the determinant of A, denoted det(A), is the area of the parallelogram formed by v₁ and v₂. If the pair is negatively oriented, then det(A) is −1 times the area of the parallelogram. For the identity, det(I) = 1; for A = [−2 0; 0 1], whose columns are negatively oriented and form a 2 × 1 rectangle, det(A) = −2. In terms of the entries, det [a b; c d] = ad − bc, which with a little bit of work can be shown to be the same signed area.

concepts.name: Determinant as a signed volume
concepts.statement: We can define determinants for n × n matrices by measuring the volume of a box defined by the columns of the matrix, even if this box resides in ℝⁿ for some very large n. The columns of a 3 × 3 matrix form a parallelepiped, and there is a means by which sets of such vectors are classified as positively or negatively oriented, so det(A) is defined in terms of the volume of the parallelepiped. If the columns are linearly dependent, the vectors cannot create a positive volume.

concepts.name: Determinant of a triangular matrix
concepts.statement: If A is a triangular matrix, then det(A) equals the product of the entries on the diagonal. For example, det [2 2; 0 3] = 2 · 3 = 6, since the parallelogram formed by its columns and the 2 × 3 rectangle have equal area; a cofactor expansion along the first row shows the same thing in general.

concepts.name: Determinant as a scaling of area
concepts.statement: Rather than simply thinking of the determinant as the area of a parallelogram, we may also think of it as a factor by which areas are scaled under the matrix transformation defined by the matrix: applying the matrix transformation defined by B scales area by det(B).

concepts.name: Determinant of a product
concepts.statement: The determinant satisfies a multiplicative property, det(AB) = det(A)det(B). Applying the matrix transformation defined by B scales area by det(B); composing with the transformation defined by A scales area a second time by det(A), so the transformation defined by AB scales area by det(A)det(B).

concepts.name: Properties of the determinant
concepts.statement: The determinant satisfies these properties: the determinant of a triangular matrix equals the product of its diagonal entries; if P is obtained by interchanging two rows of the identity matrix, then det(P) = −1, since its columns form a negatively oriented pair; and det(AB) = det(A)det(B).

forms.condition: P obtained by interchanging two rows of the identity

concepts.name: Diagonal matrix
concepts.statement: A matrix such as S = [1 0 0; 0 3 0; 0 0 1] is diagonal since its only nonzero entries are on the diagonal of the matrix. A diagonal matrix is triangular, so its determinant is the product of its diagonal entries, and scaling a row of a matrix A is performed by multiplying A by a diagonal matrix.

concepts.name: The effect of row operations on the determinant
concepts.statement: If A′ is obtained from A by scaling a row by k, then det(A′) = k det(A), since A′ = SA with S diagonal and det(S) = k. If A′ is obtained from A by interchanging two rows, then det(A′) = −det(A), since A′ = PA and det(P) = −1. If A′ is obtained from A by performing a row replacement operation, then det(A′) = det(A), since A′ = RA with R lower triangular and det(R) = 1.

forms.condition: A′ obtained from A by scaling a row by k
A′ obtained from A by interchanging two rows
A′ obtained from A by a row replacement

concepts.name: Computing a determinant with row operations
concepts.statement: Applying the forward substitution phase of Gaussian elimination to the matrix A leads to an upper triangular matrix U with A ∼ U. Keeping track of the operations used, det(A) equals det(U), the product of U's diagonal entries, multiplied by the reciprocal of each scaling factor and by −1 for each interchange; for A = [1 −1 2; −2 2 −6; 3 −1 10], two replacements and one interchange give det(A) = −det(U) = 4. This is what most computer programs do when they compute a determinant.

concepts.name: Invertibility and the determinant
concepts.statement: The matrix A is invertible if and only if det(A) ≠ 0. When the columns of A are linearly dependent, the parallelogram they form folds down onto a line and has zero area, so det(A) = 0, and linearly dependent columns is precisely the condition that A is not invertible. More fully: the forward substitution phase leads to an upper triangular U with A ∼ U; U is invertible when all of its diagonal entries are nonzero, which is also the condition that det(U) ≠ 0; row operations only multiply the determinant by a nonzero number, so det(A) ≠ 0 gives det(U) ≠ 0, U invertible, U ∼ I and A ∼ I.

forms.condition: the columns of A linearly dependent

concepts.name: Determinant of an inverse
concepts.statement: If A is an invertible matrix, then det(A⁻¹) = 1/det(A), since A⁻¹A = I tells us that det(A⁻¹A) = det(A⁻¹)det(A) = 1.

concepts.name: Cofactor expansion
concepts.statement: To find the determinant of an n × n matrix by a cofactor expansion, choose one row or column; the result is the same whichever is chosen. The determinant is a sum of terms, one for each entry in the row, each term the product of (−1)ⁱ⁺ʲ where i and j are the row and column numbers of the entry, the entry itself, and the determinant of the entries left over when the row and column containing the entry are crossed out. The choice of a row or column with zeros simplifies the computation. It is not a practical way to compute a determinant: a 10 × 10 matrix involves 10! = 3628800 terms, while Gaussian elimination takes about n³ = 1000 steps.

concepts.name: Subspace
concepts.statement: A subspace of ℝᵖ is a subset of ℝᵖ that is the span of a set of vectors. Since we have explored the concept of span in some detail, this definition just gives a new word to describe something familiar: the span of the columns of a matrix and the solution space of a homogeneous equation. The zero vector belongs to any subspace, since 0 is the linear combination with all weights zero, so a line that does not pass through the origin is not a subspace.

concepts.name: Subspaces of three-dimensional space
concepts.statement: The span of a single nonzero vector v is a line passing through the origin; the span of two linearly independent vectors v₁, v₂ is a plane passing through the origin; Span{e₁, e₂, e₃} = ℝ³; and Span{0} consists of the single vector 0. Any subspace of ℝ³ is one of these types: 0-dimensional, the origin; a 1-dimensional line; a 2-dimensional plane; or the 3-dimensional subspace ℝ³. There is no 4-dimensional subspace of ℝ³ because there is no linearly independent set of four vectors in ℝ³.

concepts.name: Basis of a subspace
concepts.statement: A basis for a subspace S of ℝᵖ is a set of vectors in S that are linearly independent and whose span is S. It is possible to represent some subspaces as the span of more than one set of vectors; we are particularly interested in representing a subspace as the span of a linearly independent set.

concepts.name: Dimension
concepts.statement: We say that the dimension of the subspace S, denoted dim S, is the number of vectors in any basis. A subspace of ℝ⁴ with a basis of two vectors is a two-dimensional subspace of ℝ⁴.

concepts.name: Finding a basis of a span
concepts.statement: To find a basis of S = Span{v₁, v₂, v₃}, row reduce the matrix [v₁ v₂ v₃]. Its reduced row echelon form shows which vectors are linear combinations of the others, such as v₂ = −v₁, so that any linear combination c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + c₃v₃ = (c₁ − c₂)v₁ + c₃v₃ and S = Span{v₁, v₃}; it also shows that the remaining vectors are linearly independent, so they form a basis for S.

concepts.name: Column space, null space, and the two fundamental questions
concepts.statement: There are two important subspaces associated to any matrix, each of which springs from one of our two fundamental questions. The column space Col(A) contains all the vectors b for which the equation Ax = b is consistent, which is the question of existence; the null space Nul(A) is the solution space of Ax = 0, which reflects on the uniqueness of solutions to this and other equations.

concepts.name: Column space
concepts.statement: If A is an m × n matrix, we call the span of its columns the column space of A and denote it as Col(A). The columns of A are vectors in ℝᵐ, so any linear combination of them is also in ℝᵐ, and Col(A) is a subspace of ℝᵐ. If A is invertible, Col(A) = ℝⁿ.

concepts.name: Rank
concepts.statement: The rank of a matrix A is the number of pivot positions in A and is denoted by rank(A). For the matrix of Example 3.5.7, the rank is two because there are two pivot positions.

concepts.name: Basis and dimension of the column space
concepts.statement: If A is an m × n matrix, then Col(A) is a subspace of ℝᵐ whose dimension equals rank(A). The columns of A that contain pivot positions form a basis for Col(A), since a column without a pivot position can be written as a linear combination of the columns that have pivot positions. We determine the pivot positions from the reduced row echelon form of A, but we form the basis from the columns of A rather than the columns of the reduced row echelon matrix.

concepts.name: Null space
concepts.statement: If A is an m × n matrix, we call the subset of vectors x in ℝⁿ satisfying Ax = 0 the null space of A and denote it by Nul(A). It is the solution space of the homogeneous equation, and the parametric description of that solution space shows that Nul(A) is the span of a set of vectors and therefore a subspace of ℝⁿ. If the columns of A are linearly independent, Nul(A) = {0}.

concepts.name: Finding a basis of the null space
concepts.statement: To find a basis for Nul(A), augment A and its reduced row echelon form by a column of zeroes, write the basic variables in terms of the free variables, and write the solution in vector form, x = x₃v₁ + x₄v₂ + x₅v₃. Any vector satisfying Ax = 0 is a linear combination of these vectors, which are linearly independent, so they form a basis for Nul(A).

concepts.name: Dimension of the null space
concepts.statement: If A is an m × n matrix, then Nul(A) is a subspace of ℝⁿ whose dimension is dim Nul(A) = n − rank(A): the dimension of Nul(A) equals the number of free variables in the equation Ax = 0, which is the number of columns of A without pivot positions.

concepts.name: Dimensions of the column space and null space
concepts.statement: If A is an m × n matrix, then dim Col(A) + dim Nul(A) = n, which follows from combining dim Col(A) = rank(A) with dim Nul(A) = n − rank(A).

concepts.name: Eigenvector
concepts.statement: Given a square n × n matrix A, we say that a nonzero vector v is an eigenvector of A if there is a scalar λ such that Av = λv. For A = [7 6; 6 −2] and v = [2, 1], Av = [20, 10] = 10v, so v is an eigenvector of A; multiplying an eigenvector by A reduces to the much simpler operation of scalar multiplying by λ.

concepts.name: Eigenvalue
concepts.statement: The scalar λ in Av = λv is called the eigenvalue associated to the eigenvector v. In Example 4.1.2, Av = 10v says that v is an eigenvector of A with associated eigenvalue λ = 10, and Aw = −5w that w is an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ = −5.

concepts.name: Geometric meaning of an eigenvector
concepts.statement: To be an eigenvector of A, the vector v must satisfy Av = λv for some scalar λ. This means that v and Av are scalar multiples of each other so they must lie on the same line. Most of the time, the vectors v and Av appear visually unrelated; for certain vectors, however, v and Av line up with one another, and we call attention to these vectors by calling them eigenvectors. For A = [1 2; 2 1], v = [1, 0] is not an eigenvector, while v = [1, 1] is, since Av is obtained from v by stretching v by a factor of 3; the matrix [0 −1; 1 0] rotates vectors by 90°, so it is not possible for v and Av to lie on the same line and it has no eigenvectors.

concepts.name: Scalar multiples of an eigenvector
concepts.statement: Any multiple of the eigenvector [1, 1] of A = [1 2; 2 1] is also an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue λ = 3: scalar multiples of an eigenvector are also eigenvectors, with the same eigenvalue. In fact, all the eigenvectors associated to a given eigenvalue form a subspace of ℝⁿ.

concepts.name: Multiplying a linear combination of eigenvectors
concepts.statement: If v₁ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 3 and v₂ an eigenvector with eigenvalue −1, so that Av₁ = 3v₁ and Av₂ = −v₂, then by the linearity of matrix multiplication A(c₁v₁ + c₂v₂) = 3c₁v₁ − c₂v₂: multiplying by A has the effect of stretching a vector x in the v₁ direction by a factor of 3 and flipping x in the v₂ direction. For x = v₁ − 2v₂ this gives Ax = 3v₁ + 2v₂.
