A{\mathbf x} = A({\mathbf v}_1 - 2{\mathbf v}_2) = 3{\mathbf v}_1 + 2{\mathbf v}_2

concepts.name: A matrix seen in a basis of eigenvectors
concepts.statement: The diagonal matrix D = [3 0; 0 −1] combines a horizontal stretching by a factor of 3 with a reflection across the horizontal axis. The matrix A = [1 2; 2 1] has a similar effect when viewed in the basis defined by its eigenvectors v₁ and v₂: it stretches by 3 in the v₁ direction and flips in the v₂ direction, so A has the same geometric effect as D when expressed in the coordinate system defined by the basis of eigenvectors.

concepts.name: Basis of eigenvectors
concepts.statement: In a sense that will be made precise later, having a set of eigenvectors of A that forms a basis of ℝ² enables us to think of A as being equivalent to a diagonal matrix D. It may not always be possible to form a basis from the eigenvectors of a matrix: the only eigenvectors of the shear [2 1; 0 2] have the form [x, 0], and the 90° rotation [0 −1; 1 0] has none. Question 4.1.8 asks: if A is an n × n matrix, can we form a basis of ℝⁿ consisting of eigenvectors of A?

concepts.name: Predicting long-term behavior with eigenvectors
concepts.statement: For the rental cars, x_{k+1} = Ax_k with A = [0.8 0.6; 0.2 0.4], whose eigenvectors are v₁ = [3, 1] with λ₁ = 1 and v₂ = [−1, 1] with λ₂ = 0.2. Writing the initial vector as a linear combination of eigenvectors, x₀ = [1000, 0] = 250v₁ − 250v₂ by row reducing the augmented matrix [v₁ v₂ | x₀], and multiplying repeatedly by A gives x_k = 250v₁ − (0.2)ᵏ250v₂. As each day goes by the second term is multiplied by 0.2, so the distribution of cars stabilizes at x = 250v₁ = [750, 250]: our understanding of the eigenvectors lets us replace matrix multiplication by scalar multiplication and look far into the future.

concepts.name: Characteristic equation
concepts.statement: An eigenvector v satisfies Av = λv, which we rewrite as Av − λIv = 0, that is, (A − λI)v = 0: an eigenvector is a nonzero solution of this homogeneous equation. Since an eigenvalue λ is a scalar for which (A − λI)v = 0 has a nonzero solution, A − λI is not invertible and its determinant is zero. This gives the equation det(A − λI) = 0, whose solutions are the eigenvalues of A; it is called the characteristic equation of A. For A = [−4 4; −12 10] it reads λ² − 6λ + 8 = (λ − 4)(λ − 2) = 0, so the eigenvalues are λ = 4 and λ = 2.

concepts.name: Characteristic polynomial
concepts.statement: The expression det(A − λI) is a polynomial in λ, called the characteristic polynomial of A. If A is an n × n matrix, its degree is n: a quadratic for a 2 × 2 matrix, a cubic for a 3 × 3. A degree n polynomial has n roots, so the characteristic equation can be written det(A − λI) = (λ₁ − λ)(λ₂ − λ)…(λₙ − λ) = 0, giving eigenvalues λ₁, λ₂, …, λₙ, some of which may be complex and some of which may appear more than once; its roots may be real and distinct, as for (4 − λ)(−2 − λ)(3 − λ) = 0, repeated, as for (2 − λ)² = 0, or complex, as for λ² + 1 = 0.

concepts.name: Eigenvalues of a triangular matrix
concepts.statement: To find the eigenvalues of a triangular matrix, we remember that the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of the entries on the diagonal: the matrix [4 2 3; 0 −2 −1; 0 0 3] has the characteristic equation (4 − λ)(−2 − λ)(3 − λ) = 0, showing that the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries λ = 4, −2, 3.

concepts.name: Complex eigenvalues
concepts.statement: Some of the roots of the characteristic polynomial, and so some of the eigenvalues, may be complex: the 90° rotation [0 −1; 1 0] has det(A − λI) = λ² + 1 = (i − λ)(−i − λ) = 0, so its eigenvalues are λ = i and λ = −i, and there is no real eigenvector. A matrix with complex eigenvalues has no basis of ℝⁿ consisting of eigenvectors, though it can still be related to a simpler matrix.

concepts.name: Eigenspace
concepts.statement: The eigenvectors associated to an eigenvalue λ are the nonzero solutions of the homogeneous equation (A − λI)v = 0; in other words, they form the null space Nul(A − λI), which shows that the eigenvectors associated to an eigenvalue form a subspace of ℝⁿ. We denote the subspace of eigenvectors of A associated to the eigenvalue λ by E_λ = Nul(A − λI) and say that E_λ is the eigenspace of A associated to the eigenvalue λ. For A = [−4 4; −12 10], E₄ is one-dimensional with basis vector [1, 2] and E₂ has basis [2, 3]; for A = −I, every vector is an eigenvector and E₋₁ = ℝ².

concepts.name: Finding the eigenvectors of an eigenvalue
concepts.statement: Once we find an eigenvalue λ of a matrix A, describing the associated eigenspace E_λ amounts to the familiar task of describing the null space Nul(A − λI): form A − λI, row reduce it, and read off a basis of its null space from the parametric description of the solutions. For A = [−4 4; −12 10] and λ = 4, A − 4I = [−8 4; −12 6] ∼ [1 −1/2; 0 0], so the eigenvectors satisfy v₁ = ½v₂ and E₄ has basis vector [1/2, 1], or [1, 2].

concepts.name: Checking eigenvalue computations
concepts.statement: If λ is a solution to the characteristic equation, then A − λI is not invertible and, consequently, A − λI must contain a row without a pivot position. This serves as a check on our work: if we row reduce A − λI and find the identity matrix, then we have made an error either in solving the characteristic equation or in finding Nul(A − λI).

concepts.name: Multiplicity of an eigenvalue
concepts.statement: Some of the eigenvalues may appear in the list λ₁, λ₂, …, λₙ more than once, so we can always write the characteristic equation in the form (λ₁ − λ)^{m₁}(λ₂ − λ)^{m₂}…(λ_p − λ)^{m_p} = 0. The number of times that λ_j − λ appears as a factor in the characteristic polynomial is called the multiplicity of the eigenvalue λ_j. The matrix [1 1; −1 3] has characteristic equation (2 − λ)² = 0 and a single eigenvalue λ = 2 of multiplicity 2; a matrix with characteristic equation (4 − λ)²(−5 − λ)(1 − λ)⁷(3 − λ)² = 0 has four eigenvalues of multiplicities 2, 1, 7 and 2, and since the degree is the sum of the multiplicities, 12, it is a 12 × 12 matrix.

concepts.name: Dimension of an eigenspace and multiplicity
concepts.statement: Proposition 4.2.9. If λ is a real eigenvalue of the matrix A with multiplicity m, then 1 ≤ dim E_λ ≤ m. The multiplicities of the eigenvalues are important because they influence the dimension of the eigenspaces: the dimension of an eigenspace must be at least one, and it can be no larger than the multiplicity of its eigenvalue. For −I, λ = −1 has multiplicity 2 and dim E₋₁ = 2; for [1 1; −1 3], λ = 2 has multiplicity 2 but dim E₂ = 1; an eigenvalue of multiplicity 1 has a one-dimensional eigenspace.

forms.condition: λ a real eigenvalue of multiplicity m

concepts.name: Distinct eigenvalues give a basis of eigenvectors
concepts.statement: Proposition 4.2.14. If A is an n × n matrix having n distinct real eigenvalues, then there is a basis of ℝⁿ consisting of eigenvectors of A. It frequently happens that the characteristic equation has the form (λ₁ − λ)(λ₂ − λ)…(λₙ − λ) = 0 with n distinct real eigenvalues, each of multiplicity 1; then each eigenspace has dimension dim E_{λ_j} = 1, and choosing a basis vector v_j for each of them produces a basis for ℝⁿ. This provides one answer to Question 4.1.8.

concepts.name: Finding eigenvalues and eigenvectors in Sage
concepts.statement: Sage finds the characteristic polynomial of A with A.charpoly('lambda') and its factored form with A.fcp('lambda'), which tells us the eigenvalues and their multiplicities; A.eigenvalues() lists the eigenvalues, an eigenvalue repeated as many times as its multiplicity; A.eigenvectors_right() returns, for each eigenvalue, a triple of the eigenvalue, a basis for E_λ and the multiplicity. Because computers perform only approximate arithmetic with decimal entries, Sage may report that A − I row reduces to the identity for A = [0.4 0.3; 0.6 0.7] even though λ = 1 is an eigenvalue; writing the entries as rational numbers, 4/10 and so on, gets around this.

concepts.name: Diagonalization
concepts.statement: Suppose we have an n × n matrix A and a basis of ℝⁿ consisting of eigenvectors v₁, v₂, …, vₙ of A with associated eigenvalues λ₁, λ₂, …, λₙ. If we use the eigenvectors to form the matrix P = [v₁ v₂ … vₙ] and the eigenvalues to form the diagonal matrix D with the λ_j on its diagonal, then AP = [Av₁ … Avₙ] = [λ₁v₁ … λₙvₙ] = PD, P is invertible since its columns form a basis, and hence A = PDP⁻¹ (Proposition 4.3.2). The expression A = PDP⁻¹ says that A, expressed in the basis defined by the columns of P, has the same geometric effect as D, expressed in the standard basis; this is the sense in which A is equivalent to a diagonal matrix. There are many ways to diagonalize A: reordering the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, or choosing a different basis for an eigenspace, gives different P and D.

concepts.name: Diagonalizable matrix
concepts.statement: We say that the matrix A is diagonalizable if there is a diagonal matrix D and invertible matrix P such that A = PDP⁻¹. A = [−5 6; −3 4] is diagonalizable, with D = [−2 0; 0 1] and P = [2 1; 1 1]; A = [0 4; −1 4], whose only eigenspace E₂ is one-dimensional, is not.

concepts.name: Diagonalizability and a basis of eigenvectors
concepts.statement: Proposition 4.3.7. An n × n matrix A is diagonalizable if and only if there is a basis of ℝⁿ consisting of eigenvectors of A. In fact, if we only know that A = PDP⁻¹, we can say that the columns of P are eigenvectors of A and that the diagonal entries of D are the associated eigenvalues: if D = [2 0; 0 −2] and P = [1 1; 1 2], then [1, 1] is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue 2 and [1, 2] one with eigenvalue −2.

concepts.name: Diagonalizing a matrix
concepts.statement: To find a diagonalization of A, if one exists, solve the characteristic equation for the eigenvalues, find a basis of each eigenspace E_λ by constructing Nul(A − λI), and check whether these basis vectors together form a basis of ℝⁿ; if they do, form D from the eigenvalues and P from the eigenvectors in the same order and verify PDP⁻¹ = A. For A = [−5 6; −3 4], the eigenvalues are λ₁ = −2 and λ₂ = 1 with eigenvectors v₁ = [2, 1] and v₂ = [1, 1], and PDP⁻¹ = [2 1; 1 1][−2 0; 0 1][1 −1; −1 2] = A. For A = [0 4; −1 4], the single eigenvalue λ = 2 has a one-dimensional eigenspace, so there is no basis of eigenvectors and A is not diagonalizable.

concepts.name: Powers of a diagonalizable matrix
concepts.statement: Proposition 4.3.9. If A = PDP⁻¹, then Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹; when A is invertible, we also have A⁻¹ = PD⁻¹P⁻¹. The powers of a diagonal matrix are found by raising its diagonal entries: for D = [2 0; 0 −1], Dᵏ = [2ᵏ 0; 0 (−1)ᵏ]. For the rental cars, A = PDP⁻¹ with P = [3 −1; 1 1] and D = [1 0; 0 0.2], so Dᵏ = [1 0; 0 0.2ᵏ] ≈ [1 0; 0 0] for large k and Aᵏ ≈ P[1 0; 0 0]P⁻¹ = [3/4 3/4; 1/4 1/4], which carries x₀ = [1000, 0] to about [750, 250].

concepts.name: Similar matrices
concepts.statement: We say that A is similar to B if there is an invertible matrix P such that A = PBP⁻¹. A matrix is diagonalizable if and only if it is similar to a diagonal matrix. The effect of multiplying a vector by A = PBP⁻¹, viewed in the basis defined by the columns of P, is the same as the effect of multiplying by B in the standard basis, and in this case Aᵏ = PBᵏP⁻¹.

concepts.name: Rotation and scaling by a complex eigenvalue
concepts.statement: Suppose a 2 × 2 matrix A has a complex eigenvalue λ = a + bi; then A is similar to C = [a −b; b a]. The point (a, b) defines r, the distance from the origin, and θ, the angle formed with the positive horizontal axis, so that a = r cos θ, b = r sin θ and r = √(a² + b²) by the Pythagorean theorem. Rewriting C = [r 0; 0 r][cos θ −sin θ; sin θ cos θ] shows that C has the geometric effect of rotating vectors by θ and scaling them by a factor of r: for λ = 1 + i, r = √2 and θ = 45°.

concepts.name: Similarity for a complex eigenvalue
concepts.statement: Proposition 4.3.12. If A is a 2 × 2 matrix with a complex eigenvalue λ = a + bi, then A is similar to C = [a −b; b a]; that is, there is a matrix P such that A = PCP⁻¹. A has the same geometric effect as C, a rotation by θ and a scaling by r, when viewed in the basis provided by the columns of P, and Aᵏ = PCᵏP⁻¹. For A = [−2 2; −5 4] with λ₁ = 1 + i, C = [1 −1; 1 1] and P = [1 1; 2 1]; choosing λ₂ = 1 − i instead gives C′ = [1 1; −1 1] and P′ = [1 −1; 2 −1]. Exercise 4.3.8 finds P from a complex eigenvector v = v₁ − iv₂ as P = [v₁ v₂].

forms.condition: A 2 × 2 with eigenvalue a + bi, C = [a −b; b a]

concepts.name: Interacting species as a dynamical system
concepts.statement: The populations of two interacting species form a dynamical system: wolves on Isle Royale prey on moose, a predator–prey relationship, while bees and flowering plants are mutually beneficial. Recording the populations in year k in a vector x_k = [R_k, S_k], the populations of the following year are x_{k+1} = Ax_k; for R_{k+1} = 0.9R_k + 0.8S_k and S_{k+1} = 0.2R_k + 0.9S_k, A = [0.9 0.8; 0.2 0.9], and each species, which would decline on its own, grows by a share of the other. In a predator–prey system such as A = [0.7 0.5; −0.4 1.6], the prey S helps the predator R to grow while R inhibits the growth of S.

concepts.name: A dynamical system in eigenvector coordinates
concepts.statement: The eigenvectors v₁ and v₂ of A form a basis 𝓑 of ℝ², which says that A is diagonalizable, A = PDP⁻¹. The coordinate system defined by 𝓑 can be used to express the state vectors: {x₀}_𝓑 = [2, 1] for x₀ = 2v₁ + v₂, and {x₁}_𝓑 = D{x₀}_𝓑, so that {x_k}_𝓑 = [1.3ᵏ·2, 0.5ᵏ·1]. More generally {Ax}_𝓑 = D{x}_𝓑, which is a restatement of the fact that A is similar to D. In 𝓑-coordinates each step scales horizontally by λ₁ = 1.3 and vertically by λ₂ = 0.5, so the points move along a curve away from the origin, ever closer to the horizontal axis; changing coordinates back, they move ever closer to the line defined by v₁. The phase portrait of D is determined only by the two eigenvalues, and that of A has a similar appearance with the eigenvectors v_j replacing the standard basis vectors e_j.

concepts.name: Trajectory
concepts.statement: Regardless of x₀, the population vectors, in the coordinates defined by 𝓑, are scaled horizontally by a factor of 1.3 and vertically by a factor of 0.5. The sequence of points {x_k}_𝓑, called trajectories, move along the curves shown; in the standard coordinate system, the trajectories x_k = Aᵏx₀ converge to the eigenspace E_1.3. Eventually the vectors become practically indistinguishable from a scalar multiple of v₁, so the ratio R_k/S_k approaches 2 and both populations are multiplied by 1.3 every year, a growth rate of about 30%, independently of the initial populations.

concepts.name: Phase portrait
concepts.statement: Diagrams showing the trajectories of a dynamical system, like those of Figure 4.4.1, are called phase portraits: on the left the phase portrait of the diagonal matrix D = [1.3 0; 0 0.5], on the right that of A = [0.9 0.8; 0.2 0.9]. The phase portrait of D is relatively easy to understand because it is determined only by the two eigenvalues; once we have it, the phase portrait of A has a similar appearance with the eigenvectors v_j replacing the standard basis vectors e_j.

concepts.name: Repellor
concepts.statement: Suppose that A has two real eigenvalues λ₁ and λ₂ and that both |λ₁|, |λ₂| > 1. In this case, any nonzero vector x₀ forms a trajectory that moves away from the origin so we say that the origin is a repellor, as for E = [1.3 0; 0 1.5].

concepts.name: Saddle
concepts.statement: Suppose that A has two real eigenvalues λ₁ and λ₂ and that |λ₁| > 1 > |λ₂|. In this case, most nonzero vectors x₀ form trajectories that converge to the eigenspace E_{λ₁}, pushed away from the origin in the direction of E_{λ₁}, and we say that the origin is a saddle, as for E = [0.7 0; 0 1.5] or the species of A = [0.9 0.8; 0.2 0.9].

concepts.name: Attractor
concepts.statement: Suppose that A has two real eigenvalues λ₁ and λ₂ and that both |λ₁|, |λ₂| < 1. In this case, any nonzero vector x₀ forms a trajectory that moves into the origin so we say that the origin is an attractor, as for E = [0.3 0; 0 0.7].

concepts.name: Spiral repellor
concepts.statement: Suppose that A has a complex eigenvalue λ = a + bi where |λ| > 1, that is, a² + b² > 1. In this case, a nonzero vector x₀ forms a trajectory that spirals away from the origin. We say that the origin is a spiral repellor, as for E = [1 −0.9; 0.9 1].

concepts.name: Center
concepts.statement: Suppose that A has a complex eigenvalue λ = a + bi where |λ| = 1, that is, a² + b² = 1. In this case, a nonzero vector x₀ forms a trajectory that moves on a closed curve around the origin. We say that the origin is a center, as for the rotation E = [0 −1; 1 0].

concepts.name: Spiral attractor
concepts.statement: Suppose that A has a complex eigenvalue λ = a + bi where |λ| < 1, that is, a² + b² < 1. In this case, a nonzero vector x₀ forms a trajectory that spirals into the origin. We say that the origin is a spiral attractor, as for E = [0.6 −0.2; 0.2 0.6].

concepts.name: Six types of dynamical systems
concepts.statement: A 2 × 2 dynamical system x_{k+1} = Ax_k is one of six types, determined by the eigenvalues of A: with two real eigenvalues, a repellor when |λ₁|, |λ₂| > 1, a saddle when |λ₁| > 1 > |λ₂|, an attractor when |λ₁|, |λ₂| < 1; with a complex eigenvalue λ = a + bi, a spiral repellor when |λ| > 1, a center when |λ| = 1, a spiral attractor when |λ| < 1. Writing A = PEP⁻¹, the phase portrait of E is drawn in the eigenvector coordinates and that of A follows with the columns of P in place of e₁, e₂. There are other possibilities if, for instance, one of the eigenvalues is 0, and the next section explores the situation when one of the eigenvalues is 1.

concepts.name: Dynamical systems in three or more dimensions
concepts.statement: The general case is quite similar to the 2 × 2 one. For a 3 × 3 system whose matrix has eigenvalues λ₁ = 0.6, λ₂ = 0.8 and λ₃ = 1.1, real and distinct, there is a basis 𝓑 of eigenvectors, and in its coordinate system all the trajectories {x_k}_𝓑 converge into the eigenspace E_1.1. With complex eigenvalues λ = 0.8 ± 0.5i, |λ| < 1, and λ₃ = 1.1, there is a two-dimensional subspace in which the trajectories spiral in toward the origin while, once again, they all converge into E_1.1. The same kind of reasoning allows us to analyze n × n systems, such as the three age groups of a bison herd, whose growth rate is the real eigenvalue larger than 1.

concepts.name: Probability vector
concepts.statement: A vector whose entries are nonnegative and add to 1 is called a probability vector. The vector x₀ = [0.4, 0.3, 0.3] of the percentages of voters choosing three parties is a probability vector, since every voter votes for one of the three parties; the entries of the matrix of a Markov chain are probabilities, between 0 and 1.

concepts.name: Stochastic matrix
concepts.statement: A square matrix whose columns are probability vectors is called a stochastic matrix. The rental car matrix A = [0.8 0.4; 0.2 0.6] is stochastic: each entry is the probability that a car rented at one location is returned to another, and since a car rented at one location must be returned to one of the locations, the entries in each column add to 1.

concepts.name: Markov chain
concepts.statement: If we have a stochastic matrix A and a probability vector x₀, we can form the sequence x_k where x_{k+1} = Ax_k. We call this sequence of vectors a Markov chain; the vectors x_k are all probability vectors (Exercise 4.5.6). We may think of the sequence as describing the evolution of some conserved quantity, such as the number of rental cars or voters, among a number of possible states over time: for the voters, x₁ = [0.300, 0.400, 0.300], x₂ = [0.240, 0.420, 0.340], …, x₁₀ = [0.200, 0.400, 0.400].

forms.condition: A stochastic, x₀ a probability vector

concepts.name: Steady-state vector
concepts.statement: If A is a stochastic matrix, we say that a probability vector q is a steady-state or stationary vector if Aq = q. The voting Markov chain converges to q = [0.2, 0.4, 0.4], a probability vector in the eigenspace E₁ that is unchanged under multiplication by A: after a long time, 20% of voters choose party P, 40% choose Q and 40% choose R.

forms.condition: A stochastic, q a probability vector

concepts.name: Finding a steady-state vector
concepts.statement: Since λ₁ = 1 is an eigenvalue, a steady-state vector is a probability vector in the eigenspace E₁ = Nul(A − I). We find it by finding the appropriate scalar multiple of a basis vector v of E₁: for the voting matrix, v = [1, 2, 2] and cv = [c, 2c, 2c] is a probability vector when c + 2c + 2c = 5c = 1, so c = 1/5 and q = [0.2, 0.4, 0.4] is the unique probability vector in E₁. For B = [0.4 0.3; 0.6 0.7], E₁ has basis [1, 2] and q = [1/3, 2/3].

concepts.name: Eigenvalues of a stochastic matrix
concepts.statement: A few important facts about the eigenvalues of a stochastic matrix: λ = 1 is an eigenvalue of any stochastic matrix (Exercise 4.5.8), and we usually order the eigenvalues so that λ₁ = 1; all other eigenvalues satisfy |λ_j| ≤ 1; and any stochastic matrix has at least one steady-state vector q. For the voting matrix, λ₁ = 1 and λ₂, λ₃ = 0.4 ± 0.2i with |λ₂| = |λ₃| < 1, so the trajectories x_k spiral into the eigenspace E₁ and converge to the probability vector q there.

concepts.name: Convergence of a Markov chain
concepts.statement: The eigenvalues of a stochastic matrix tell us whether a Markov chain will converge to a steady-state vector (Question 4.5.3). A Markov chain could fail to converge if |λ₂| = 1: for A = [0 1; 1 0], with eigenvalues 1 and −1, the chain from x₀ = [1, 0] alternates [1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], … and converges to nothing. However, if all but the first eigenvalue satisfy |λ_j| < 1, then there is a unique steady-state vector q and any Markov chain will converge to q, as for B = [0.4 0.3; 0.6 0.7] with eigenvalues 1 and 0.1, whose chains converge to q = [1/3, 2/3].

concepts.name: Positive matrix
concepts.statement: We say that a matrix A is positive if either A or some power Aᵏ has all positive entries. The matrix [0 1; 1 0] is not positive, since every power of it has some zero entries; B = [0.4 0.3; 0.6 0.7] is positive because every entry is positive; C = [0 0.5; 1 0.5] has a zero entry, but C² = [0.5 0.25; 0.5 0.75] has all positive entries, so C is a positive matrix.

concepts.name: Perron-Frobenius theorem
concepts.statement: Theorem 4.5.6 (Perron-Frobenius). If A is a positive stochastic matrix, then the eigenvalues satisfy λ₁ = 1 and |λ_j| < 1 for j > 1. This means that A has a unique positive, steady-state vector q and that every Markov chain defined by A will converge to q. It is a simple condition on the matrix A that guarantees convergence without computing the eigenvalues; where A is not positive, as for D = [0 0.5 0; 1 0.5 0; 0 0 1], the theorem tells us nothing, and indeed D has two steady-state vectors and different Markov chains converge to different vectors.

concepts.name: PageRank algorithm
concepts.statement: Google's idea is to use the structure of the Internet to assess the quality of web pages without any human intervention: if a web page has quality content, other web pages will link to it, and a page has even higher quality if those links come from pages that are themselves assessed to have high quality. Simply said, if many quality pages link to a page, that page must itself be of high quality. This is the essence of the PageRank algorithm, in which each page divides its PageRank into equal pieces, one for each outgoing link, and gives one piece to each of the pages it links to, a page's PageRank being the sum of all the PageRank it receives; Markov chains and the Perron-Frobenius theorem are its central ingredients.

concepts.name: Google matrix
concepts.statement: The PageRank x_j of page j is determined by the rule that each page divides its PageRank equally among its outgoing links: for the three-page Internet, x₁ = x₂ + ½x₃, x₂ = ½x₁ + ½x₃, x₃ = ½x₁. Forming the PageRank vector x, these expressions take the form Gx = x, where the matrix G is called the Google matrix; its entries are nonnegative and its columns add to 1, so G is a stochastic matrix. For that Internet, G = [0 1 1/2; 1/2 0 1/2; 1/2 0 0].

concepts.name: PageRank vector
concepts.statement: Since the PageRank vector x is defined by the equation Gx = x, any vector in the eigenspace E₁ satisfies this equation; so that we might work with a specific vector, we define the PageRank vector to be the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix G. For the three-page Internet, E₁ is spanned by [4, 3, 2] and the PageRank vector is q = [4/9, 3/9, 2/9]: page 1, whose PageRank is largest, is assessed to have the highest quality.

concepts.name: Finding the PageRank vector by a Markov chain
concepts.statement: There are two ways to find the PageRank vector. The first determines a steady-state vector directly by describing the eigenspace E₁, which means finding the null space Nul(G − I); the real Internet has 35 trillion pages, so this requires row reducing a matrix with 35 trillion rows and columns, which is not computationally feasible. The second uses a Markov chain x_{k+1} = Gx_k that converges to the PageRank vector: since multiplying a vector by a matrix is significantly less work than row reducing the matrix, this approach is feasible, and it is, in fact, how Google computes the PageRank vector.

concepts.name: Modified Google matrix
concepts.statement: A Markov chain defined by G converges to a unique steady-state vector when G is positive, which fails for the cyclic five-page Internet, whose chain never settles, and for the eight-page Internet in which the pages outside a box give up all of their PageRank to the pages inside it. Google solves this problem by modifying G to obtain a positive matrix G′: thinking of the entries of G as the probability that a user follows a link, we allow the user to jump to any of the n pages with a small probability, through the positive stochastic matrix Hₙ all of whose entries are 1/n, and mix the two with a parameter α, G′ = αG + (1 − α)Hₙ. Google is thought to use α = 0.85, so G′ = 0.85G + 0.15Hₙ: a user follows a link 85% of the time and jumps to any page 15% of the time. Since G′ is positive, the Perron-Frobenius theorem tells us that any Markov chain converges to a unique steady-state vector, the PageRank vector.

concepts.name: Round off error
concepts.statement: Computers do not perform arithmetic operations exactly. They compute in base 2, so a number such as 0.1, simple in decimal form, has the repeating base-2 expansion 0.000110011001100… and can only be held approximately; and the operations themselves are prone to error: a computer keeping three decimal digits represents 1.023 as 1.02 and 0.023421 as 0.0234, and reports their sum 1.046421 as 1.04, whose last digit is not correctly rounded. This problem, called round off error, appears whenever we add numbers of significantly different magnitudes. Gaussian elimination on a 1000 × 1000 matrix requires roughly a billion operations, and the errors introduced in each could accumulate; we can never completely avoid them, but we can take steps to mitigate them.

forms.condition: a computer keeping three decimal digits, for 1.023 + 0.023421 = 1.046421

concepts.name: Sensitivity of a solution to small errors
concepts.statement: The order of the equations has no effect on the solution space, but when arithmetic is only approximate, interchanging equations can dramatically improve the accuracy of the approximate solution. For 0.0001x + y = 1, x + y = 2 the exact solution is x = 1.00010001…, y = 0.99989998…, and a three-digit computer can at best find x ≈ 1.00, y ≈ 1.00. Either order gives y ≈ 1.00; the difference comes when y is substituted into the first equation. Each equation is a line and the solution their intersection; along the nearly horizontal line 0.0001x + y = 1 a small change in y leads to a large change in x, so the slight error in y gives x ≈ 0.00, while along the line x + y = 2 of slope −1 a small change in y changes x only a little, so x ≈ 1.00. Simply interchanging the order of the equations produces a much more accurate solution.

forms.condition: the exact solution of 0.0001x + y = 1, x + y = 2
a three-digit computer, the equations in their original order and interchanged

concepts.name: Partial pivoting
concepts.statement: Computing exactly, we only need to perform a row interchange when a zero occurs in a pivot position. Computers instead perform a row interchange at each step to put the entry having the largest possible absolute value into the pivot position: for the matrix with first column 2, 1, −3, Gaussian elimination begins by interchanging the first and third rows so that the upper left entry has the largest possible absolute value. This technique is called partial pivoting, and it means that, in practice, many more row interchanges are performed than when computing by hand; it is what Sage's LU command uses.

forms.condition: the first step, interchanging rows so that the pivot has the largest absolute value

concepts.name: Finding an LU factorization
concepts.statement: To factor A as a product of two triangular matrices, A = LU with L lower triangular and U upper triangular, apply the Gaussian elimination algorithm without partial pivoting and represent each row replacement by an elementary matrix, so that E₃E₂E₁A = U is upper triangular. Then A = (E₃E₂E₁)⁻¹U = E₁⁻¹E₂⁻¹E₃⁻¹U = LU, and L is lower triangular because the elementary matrices E₁, E₂, E₃ of row replacements are. For A = [2 −3 1; −4 5 0; 2 −2 2], L = [1 0 0; −2 1 0; 1 −1 1] and U = [2 −3 1; 0 −1 2; 0 0 3].

forms.condition: the row replacements of Gaussian elimination, without partial pivoting

concepts.name: Forward substitution
concepts.statement: Because L is lower triangular, the equation Lc = b is solved by reading the components of c off one at a time from the top: for L = [1 0 0; −2 1 0; 1 −1 1] and b = [8, −13, 8], the first equation gives c₁ = 8, then −2c₁ + c₂ = −13 gives c₂ = 3, and c₁ − c₂ + c₃ = 8 gives c₃ = 3. Solving a triangular system is simplified because we only need to perform a sequence of substitutions, working downward for a lower triangular matrix as back substitution works upward for an upper triangular one.

concepts.name: Solving a system with an LU factorization
concepts.statement: An LU factorization allows us to trade in one equation Ax = b for two simpler equations: writing Ax = L(Ux) = b and defining the unknown vector c = Ux, we first solve Lc = b by forward substitution and then Ux = c by back substitution. In Example 5.1.1, c = [8, 3, 3] and x = [2, −1, 1]. To solve Ax = b for a different right-hand side b, we simply repeat the two-step process with the same L and U.

concepts.name: Efficiency of the LU factorization
concepts.statement: Solving an equation with an n × n triangular matrix requires approximately ½n² operations, so once we have A = LU, solving Ax = b by the two triangular equations takes about n² operations: for a 1000 × 1000 matrix, about one million steps against the roughly a billion, ⅔n³, that Gaussian elimination needs. Finding the LU factorization requires roughly the same amount of work as Gaussian elimination, but once we have it we can use it to solve Ax = b for different right-hand sides b without performing the elimination again.

forms.condition: operations to solve Ax = b once A = LU is known, against ⅔n³ for Gaussian elimination
operations to solve one equation with an n × n triangular matrix

concepts.name: LU factorization with a permutation matrix
concepts.statement: Gaussian elimination sometimes requires row interchanges in addition to row replacements, and a row interchange is represented by a permutation matrix such as P = [0 0 1; 0 1 0; 1 0 0], which is not triangular and so disrupts the structure of the factorization. Linear algebra software packages therefore provide a permutation matrix P that describes how the rows are permuted in the Gaussian elimination process, and write PA = LU with L lower triangular and U upper triangular; Sage's P, L, U = A.LU() returns them, found with partial pivoting. To solve Ax = b, multiply both sides by P to obtain PAx = LUx = Pb, then solve Lc = Pb and Ux = c.

forms.condition: P a permutation matrix, L lower triangular, U upper triangular

concepts.name: Why eigenvalues are not computed exactly in practice
concepts.statement: We have found the eigenvalues of a square matrix A as the roots of the characteristic polynomial det(A − λI) = 0 and the eigenvectors as the null space Nul(A − λI). This is not practical for large matrices: finding the characteristic polynomial of a large matrix requires considerable computation, as does finding the roots of that polynomial, and finding the null space of a singular matrix is plagued by numerical problems, since round off error can make A − λI appear to have a pivot in every row, as when Sage reports the reduced row echelon form of A − I as the identity for a positive stochastic matrix A. For this reason, the power method finds numerical approximations to the eigenvalues and eigenvectors instead.

concepts.name: Dominant eigenvalue
concepts.statement: The eigenvalue of a matrix A having the largest absolute value is called the dominant eigenvalue. For the positive stochastic matrix [0.7 0.6; 0.3 0.4], with eigenvalues 1 and 0.1, the dominant eigenvalue is λ₁ = 1; for [2 1; 1 2], with eigenvalues 3 and 1, it is λ₁ = 3; for [−5.1 5.7; −3.8 4.4] it is λ₁ = −1.3, since |−1.3| > |0.6|.

concepts.name: Repeated multiplication approaches the dominant eigenspace
concepts.statement: Beginning with a vector x₀ and defining the sequence x_{k+1} = Ax_k, so that x_k = Aᵏx₀, the vectors x_k become increasingly close in direction to the eigenspace of the dominant eigenvalue. If x₀ = c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ with λ₁ dominant, then x_k = c₁λ₁ᵏv₁ + c₂λ₂ᵏv₂, and the contribution of v₂ shrinks relative to v₁'s: for the stochastic matrix of Example 5.2.1, x_k = ⅓v₁ − ⅓(0.1)ᵏv₂ ≈ ⅓v₁ when k is large, which is the convergence of a Markov chain to its steady-state vector restated, and essentially how PageRank finds a basis vector of E₁; for A = [2 1; 1 2], x_k = 3ᵏ½v₁ − ½v₂ is stretched by 3 in the v₁ direction and not at all in the v₂ direction, so the vectors become increasingly long but their direction becomes closer to that of v₁ = [1, 1].

concepts.name: Power method
concepts.statement: To find an eigenvector associated to the dominant eigenvalue, we prevent the length of the vectors x_k from growing arbitrarily large by scaling: given x_k, identify its component having the largest absolute value, call it m_k, and define x̄_k = (1/m_k)x_k, whose component of largest absolute value is 1; then form x_{k+1} = Ax̄_k and repeat. Beginning with x₀ = [1, 0] and A = [2 1; 1 2], x₁ = [2, 1] with m₁ = 2 gives x̄₁ = [1, 1/2], then x₂ = Ax̄₁ = [5/2, 2] with m₂ = 5/2 gives x̄₂ = [1, 4/5], and the vectors x̄_k approach the eigenvector v₁ = [1, 1]. This is the power method for finding an eigenvector associated to the dominant eigenvalue of a matrix; the Sage command power(A, x0, N) prints m and x̄_k for N steps.

forms.condition: m_k the component of x_k having the largest absolute value

concepts.name: The multipliers approach the dominant eigenvalue
concepts.statement: The power method gives not only an eigenvector v but also its associated eigenvalue: the multipliers m_k approach the eigenvalue λ having the largest absolute value. For A = [−5.1 5.7; −3.8 4.4] with eigenvector v = [3, 2], scaling by ⅓ gives v̄ = [1, 2/3] and Av̄ = [−1.30, −0.86], whose first component still has the largest absolute value, so the multiplier m = −1.3 is the eigenvalue corresponding to the eigenvector; in Activity 5.2.2 the multipliers converge to 0.9 and to 1.3 in absolute value.

forms.condition: λ₁ the dominant eigenvalue, as k grows

concepts.name: Choice of the initial vector
concepts.statement: The power method requires us to choose an initial vector x₀. For most choices it finds the eigenvalue having the largest absolute value, but an unfortunate choice may not: had we chosen x₀ = v₂, the vectors x_k = Aᵏx₀ = λ₂ᵏv₂ would never detect the eigenvector v₁. It usually happens, however, that our initial guess x₀ has some contribution from v₁ that enables us to find it.

concepts.name: Inverse power method
concepts.statement: The eigenvectors of A are the same as those of A⁻¹: if Av = λv, then multiplying by A⁻¹ and λ⁻¹ gives A⁻¹v = λ⁻¹v, so λ⁻¹ is an eigenvalue of A⁻¹. Since |λ₂| < |λ₁| gives |λ₂⁻¹| > |λ₁⁻¹|, the eigenvalue of A having the smallest absolute value is the reciprocal of the dominant eigenvalue of A⁻¹, and the power method applied to A⁻¹ finds it, together with an eigenvector. Computing A⁻¹ is not efficient, so instead of x_{k+1} = A⁻¹x_k we solve Ax_{k+1} = x_k at each step, which an LU factorization of A makes cheap for many right-hand sides; the multipliers 1/m_k approximate the eigenvalue of A. For [−5.1 5.7; −3.8 4.4] the inverse power method gives λ₂ = 0.6 with eigenvector [1, 1]; if A is not invertible, its eigenvalue of smallest absolute value is 0.

forms.condition: solved in place of x_{k+1} = A⁻¹x_k

concepts.name: Finding the eigenvalue closest to a number
concepts.statement: The absolute value of a number is its distance from 0, so the inverse power method finds the eigenvalue closest to 0; one more modification finds all the eigenvalues. If Av = λv, then (A − sI)v = (λ − s)v for any scalar s, so v is an eigenvector of A − sI with eigenvalue λ − s, and the eigenvalue of A closest to s is the eigenvalue of A − sI closest to 0. Applying the inverse power method to A − sI therefore gives the eigenvalue of A closest to s, as 1/m_k + s, with an eigenvector; the Sage command find_closest_eigenvalue(A, s, x, N) does this. For the 4 × 4 matrix of Activity 5.2.4, the power and inverse power methods give λ₁ = 16.35 and λ₂ = 0.75, the other eigenvalues lie between −λ₁ and λ₁ (Figure 5.2.3), and probing s = −10 and s = 10 finds −4.823 and 7.526. The technique assumes that the eigenvalues of A are real and distinct.

forms.condition: m_k the multipliers of the inverse power method applied to A − sI

concepts.name: When the power method fails
concepts.statement: The power method as presented assumes that the eigenvalues of A are real and distinct, and it fails for certain unlucky matrices. When two eigenvalues have the same absolute value, as for [0 −1; −4 0] with eigenvalues 2 and −2, neither the power method nor the inverse power method converges, and looking for the eigenvalue closest to some other number breaks the symmetry; when the dominant eigenvalue is negative and the largest component changes place from step to step, as for [1 2; 2 1] under the inverse power method, the vectors x̄_k flip sign and the multipliers converge to the wrong value, which a fixed component's ratio corrects; a complex eigenvalue rotates the vectors at every step so they never converge; a repeated eigenvalue with a one-dimensional eigenspace, as for [1 1; 0 1], is still found, and two different eigenvectors found for the same eigenvalue show that its eigenspace has dimension greater than one. If A has repeated or complex eigenvalues, the technique needs to be modified.

concepts.name: Dot product
concepts.statement: For two m-dimensional vectors v and w, the dot product v·w is the scalar v₁w₁ + v₂w₂ + … + v_mw_m. The two vectors are combined in such a way as to create a number, and this number conveys useful geometric information: it helps us measure the length of vectors and the angle formed by a pair of vectors. For instance, [2, −3]·[4, 1] = 2·4 + (−3)·1 = 5, and the dot product of the four-dimensional vectors [2, 0, −3, 1] and [−1, 3, 1, 2] is 2(−1) + 0(3) + (−3)(1) + 1(2) = −3.

{\mathbf v}\cdot{\mathbf w} = \left[\begin{array}{r}v_1 \\ v_2 \end{array}\right]\cdot\left[\begin{array}{r}w_1 \\ w_2 \end{array}\right] = v_1w_1 + v_2w_2

concepts.name: Properties of the dot product
concepts.statement: As with ordinary multiplication, the dot product enjoys some familiar algebraic properties, such as commutativity and distributivity. It doesn't matter in which order we compute the dot product of two vectors, v·w = w·v; if s is a scalar, (sv)·w = s(v·w); and we may distribute the dot product across linear combinations, (c₁v₁ + c₂v₂)·w = c₁v₁·w + c₂v₂·w. If v₁·w = 4 and v₂·w = −7, then (−3v₁ + 2v₂)·w = −3(4) + 2(−7) = −26.

forms.latex: (c_1{\mathbf v}_1+c_2{\mathbf v}_2)\cdot{\mathbf w} = c_1{\mathbf v}_1\cdot{\mathbf w} + c_2{\mathbf v}_2\cdot{\mathbf w}

concepts.name: Length of a vector
concepts.statement: The length of a vector v, which we denote as |v|, may be found using the Pythagorean theorem: the vector v = [3, 2] forms the hypotenuse of a right triangle having a horizontal leg of length 3 and a vertical leg of length 2, so |v| = √(3² + 2²) = √13. The dot product of v with itself is v·v = 3(3) + 2(2) = 13 = |v|², and this is true in general: v·v = |v|².

concepts.name: Dot product and the angle between vectors
concepts.statement: The dot product of two vectors records information about the angle between them. Applying the Law of Cosines to the triangle formed by v, w and w − v, |w − v|² = |v|² + |w|² − 2|v||w| cos θ, and writing each length as a dot product, the upshot is that v·w = |v||w| cos θ, where θ is the angle between v and w. Together with v·v = |v|², this is the geometric information the dot product gives us; the angle between v and w is θ = arccos(v·w / (|v||w|)).

forms.latex: \left|{\mathbf w}-{\mathbf v}\right|^2 = \left|{\mathbf v}\right|^2 + \left|{\mathbf w}\right|^2 - 2\left|{\mathbf v}\right|\left|{\mathbf w}\right|\cos\theta

concepts.name: Orthogonal vectors
concepts.statement: When vectors v and w are perpendicular, the angle between them is θ = 90° and v·w = |v||w| cos 90° = 0, so the dot product between perpendicular vectors must be zero. We say that vectors v and w are orthogonal if v·w = 0. In practical terms, two perpendicular vectors are orthogonal; the concept of orthogonality is somewhat more general because it allows one or both of the vectors to be the zero vector 0.

concepts.name: Similarity of vectors
concepts.statement: The dot product also provides a way to compare vectors. The vectors v and w of Figure 6.1.8 seem somewhat similar as the directions they define are nearly the same, while u appears rather dissimilar to both. We measure the similarity of vectors by finding the angle between them: the smaller the angle, the more similar the vectors. Vectors formed from the word counts of Wikipedia articles are compared this way, two articles on the same subject giving nearly parallel vectors, and the correlation of two time series is the cosine of the angle between the demeaned series.

concepts.name: Distance between data points
concepts.statement: To find clusters in a dataset, we view the data points as vectors so that the distance between two data points equals the length of the vector joining them. That is, if two points are represented by the vectors v and w, then the distance between the points is |v − w|.

concepts.name: Clustering
concepts.statement: A typical problem in data science is to find some underlying patterns in a dataset. The 177 data points of Figure 6.1.10 are not scattered around haphazardly; instead, they seem to form clusters. If there are many attributes for each data point, as with medical data describing a group of patients, the data may be high-dimensional and not easily visualized, so we would like an algorithm that separates the data points into clusters without human intervention. We call the result a clustering.

concepts.name: Centroid
concepts.statement: The centroid, or the average, of a set of vectors v₁, v₂, …, vₙ is (1/n)(v₁ + v₂ + … + vₙ). The centroid lies in the center of the points defined by the vectors: the centroid of [1, 1], [4, 1] and [4, 4] is c = [3, 2].

forms.condition: the centroid of v₁, v₂, …, vₙ

concepts.name: k-means clustering
concepts.statement: To break the data points into k clusters, choose k points c₁, c₂, …, c_k at random from the dataset; construct the cluster C₁ as the set of data points closest to c₁, C₂ as the set of data points closest to c₂, and so forth; then repeat until the clusters no longer change: find the centroids c₁, c₂, …, c_k of the current clusters and update the clusters C₁, C₂, …, C_k. The clusterings we find depend on the initial random choice of points: for the four points of Activity 6.1.4, the initial choice c₁ = v₂, c₂ = v₃ leads to C₁ = {v₁}, C₂ = {v₂, v₃, v₄}, while c₁ = v₃, c₂ = v₄ leads to C₁ = {v₁, v₂, v₃}, C₂ = {v₄}.

forms.latex: \begin{array}{rcl} C_1 & {}={} & \{{\mathbf v}_1\} \\ C_2 & {}={} & \{{\mathbf v}_2, {\mathbf v}_3,{\mathbf v}_4\} \end{array}
forms.condition: the initial choice c₁ = v₂, c₂ = v₃

forms.latex: \begin{array}{rcl} C_1 & {}={} & \{{\mathbf v}_1, {\mathbf v}_2, {\mathbf v}_3\} \\ C_2 & {}={} & \{{\mathbf v}_4\} \end{array}
forms.condition: the initial choice c₁ = v₃, c₂ = v₄

concepts.name: Objective of a clustering
concepts.statement: To determine which of two clusterings is the better, we define a function, called the objective, which measures the average of the square of the distance from each point to the centroid of the cluster to which that point belongs. A clustering with a smaller objective will have clusters more tightly centered around their centroids, which should result in a better clustering. For the clustering C₁ = {v₁, v₂, v₃}, C₂ = {v₄} with centroids c₁ = [0, 4/3] and c₂ = v₄ = [3, 2], the objective is ¼(|v₁ − c₁|² + |v₂ − c₁|² + |v₃ − c₁|² + |v₄ − c₂|²) = 5/3, while the clustering C₁ = {v₁}, C₂ = {v₂, v₃, v₄} has the smaller objective 5/6 and is the tighter.

forms.condition: the clustering C₁ = {v₁, v₂, v₃}, C₂ = {v₄}

concepts.name: Choosing the number of clusters
concepts.statement: For a given value of k, our strategy is to run the algorithm several times and choose the clustering with the smallest objective, since different random choices lead to different clusterings. Plotting the minimal objective against k gives an elbow plot: the objective decreases sharply when k is small and then flattens out, and the location where it transitions from being sharply decreasing to relatively flat, the elbow, is a good choice for k, since increasing k beyond it does not significantly decrease the objective. We could increase k until each data point is its own cluster, but this defeats the point of the technique, which is to group together nearby data points in the hope that they share common features. We don't claim to have found the best clustering; the true test is how it helps us understand the dataset and make predictions about new data.

concepts.name: Orthogonal complement
concepts.statement: Given a subspace W of ℝᵐ, the orthogonal complement of W is the set of vectors in ℝᵐ each of which is orthogonal to every vector in W. We denote the orthogonal complement by W⊥. The set of scalar multiples of a vector v describes a line L, a 1-dimensional subspace of ℝ², and the vectors orthogonal to v form a second line, every vector of which is orthogonal to every vector on L: the orthogonal complement L⊥. A plane W, a two-dimensional subspace of ℝ³, has as its orthogonal complement W⊥ a line in ℝ³.

concepts.name: The orthogonal complement is a subspace
concepts.statement: The orthogonal complement of a subspace W is itself a subspace of ℝᵐ. If w₁ and w₂ form a basis for W, any vector w in W can be written as a linear combination w = c₁w₁ + c₂w₂, and if x is orthogonal to both w₁ and w₂, the distributive property of dot products gives (c₁w₁ + c₂w₂)·x = c₁w₁·x + c₂w₂·x = 0, so x is orthogonal to w. Since every vector in W⊥ is orthogonal to every vector in W, the orthogonal complement of W⊥ is W.

forms.latex: (c_1{\mathbf w}_1+c_2{\mathbf w}_2)\cdot{\mathbf x} = c_1{\mathbf w}_1\cdot{\mathbf x} + c_2{\mathbf w}_2\cdot{\mathbf x} = 0
forms.condition: x orthogonal to w₁ and w₂

concepts.name: Finding an orthogonal complement
concepts.statement: To describe W⊥ when w₁, w₂, …, wₙ is a basis for W, require that x be orthogonal to each basis vector: the equations w₁·x = 0, …, wₙ·x = 0 form a linear system Bx = 0, and its solutions, described parametrically, make up W⊥. For the line L defined by v = [1, −2, 3] in ℝ³, v·x = x₁ − 2x₂ + 3x₃ = 0 gives x = x₂[2, 1, 0] + x₃[−3, 0, 1], so L⊥ is a plane, a two-dimensional subspace spanned by [2, 1, 0] and [−3, 0, 1]. For the 2-dimensional subspace W of ℝ⁵ with basis w₁ = [−1, −2, 2, 3, −4], w₂ = [2, 4, 2, 0, 2], the system Bx = 0 has the solutions x = x₂[−2, 1, 0, 0, 0] + x₄[1, 0, −1, 1, 0] + x₅[−2, 0, 1, 0, 1], so W⊥ is a 3-dimensional subspace with basis v₁, v₂, v₃, each orthogonal to both w₁ and w₂.

forms.condition: the line defined by v = [1, −2, 3], Example 6.2.4

concepts.name: Transpose
concepts.statement: The transpose of the m × n matrix A is the n × m matrix Aᵀ whose rows are the columns of A. If A = [4 −3 0 5; −1 2 1 3], then Aᵀ = [4 −1; −3 2; 0 1; 5 3]. This new matrix operation makes explicit the connection between the orthogonal complement of a subspace and the solution set of a linear system.

concepts.name: Transpose times a vector as dot products
concepts.statement: If A is the matrix whose columns are v₁, v₂, …, vₙ, then Aᵀx = [v₁·x; v₂·x; …; vₙ·x] (Proposition 6.2.8): the components of the product Aᵀx are simply the dot products of the columns of A with x. We make frequent use of this observation. Viewing a vector as a matrix having one column, x·y = xᵀy, so that x·(Ay) = (Aᵀx)·y.

forms.latex: A^T{\mathbf x} = \begin{bmatrix} {\mathbf v}_1\cdot{\mathbf x} \\ {\mathbf v}_2\cdot{\mathbf x} \\ \vdots \\ {\mathbf v}_n\cdot{\mathbf x} \end{bmatrix}
forms.condition: A the matrix whose columns are v₁, v₂, …, vₙ
a vector viewed as a matrix having one column (Exercise 6.2.9)

concepts.name: Orthogonal complement of the column space
concepts.statement: For any matrix A, the orthogonal complement of Col(A) is Nul(Aᵀ); that is, Col(A)⊥ = Nul(Aᵀ) (Proposition 6.2.10). If the columns w₁, w₂ of A form a basis of W, then W = Col(A), and a vector x is in W⊥ exactly when Aᵀx = [w₁·x; w₂·x] = 0, so describing W⊥ is the familiar task of describing the solution set of Aᵀx = 0, which is the null space of Aᵀ.

forms.latex: A^T{\mathbf x} = \left[\begin{array}{r}{\mathbf w}_1\cdot{\mathbf x} \\ {\mathbf w}_2\cdot{\mathbf x} \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]
forms.condition: x in W⊥, A = [w₁ w₂], Example 6.2.9

concepts.name: Transpose of a product
concepts.statement: If AB is defined, then (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ. Notice that the order of the multiplication is reversed; the product AᵀBᵀ need not even be defined, as when A is 2 × 3 and B is 3 × 4.

concepts.name: Determinant of the transpose
concepts.statement: If C is a square matrix, then det(C) = det(Cᵀ).

concepts.name: Properties of the transpose
concepts.statement: The transpose satisfies these properties, expressed in terms of general matrices A, B and a square matrix C: if A + B is defined, then (A + B)ᵀ = Aᵀ + Bᵀ; (sA)ᵀ = sAᵀ; (Aᵀ)ᵀ = A; Iᵀ = I; and if C is invertible, then Cᵀ is invertible and (Cᵀ)⁻¹ = (C⁻¹)ᵀ, since (CC⁻¹)ᵀ = (C⁻¹)ᵀCᵀ = Iᵀ = I.

concepts.name: Rank of the transpose
concepts.statement: For any matrix A, we have rank(A) = rank(Aᵀ) (Proposition 6.2.12). Why this is true is explained in Section 7.4; it is important because it implies a relationship between the dimensions of a subspace and its orthogonal complement.

concepts.name: Dimension of the orthogonal complement
concepts.statement: If W is a subspace of ℝᵐ, then dim W + dim W⊥ = m (Proposition 6.2.13). If W is n-dimensional with basis w₁, w₂, …, wₙ and A = [w₁ w₂ … wₙ], then Col(A) = W so that rank(A) = dim Col(A) = dim W = n; the transpose Aᵀ is an n × m matrix having rank(Aᵀ) = rank(A) = n, and since W⊥ = Nul(Aᵀ), dim W⊥ = dim Nul(Aᵀ) = m − rank(Aᵀ) = m − n = m − dim W. The orthogonal complement of a line in ℝ³ has dimension 3 − 1 = 2, which explains why it is a plane, and that of a 2-dimensional subspace of ℝ⁵ is 5 − 2 = 3-dimensional.

forms.condition: A = [w₁ w₂ … wₙ], a basis of W

concepts.name: Orthogonal set
concepts.statement: By an orthogonal set of vectors, we mean a set of nonzero vectors each of which is orthogonal to the others. The 3-dimensional vectors w₁ = [1, −1, 1], w₂ = [1, 1, 0], w₃ = [1, −1, −2] form an orthogonal set, which can be verified by computing w₁·w₂ = 0, w₁·w₃ = 0, w₂·w₃ = 0, and this set forms a basis for ℝ³; three orthogonal 4-dimensional vectors form a basis for a 3-dimensional subspace W of ℝ⁴ rather than for ℝ⁴.

forms.latex: \begin{array}{rcl} {\mathbf w}_1\cdot{\mathbf w}_2 & {}={} & 0 \\ {\mathbf w}_1\cdot{\mathbf w}_3 & {}={} & 0 \\ {\mathbf w}_2\cdot{\mathbf w}_3 & {}={} & 0 \end{array}

concepts.name: Weights of a linear combination of an orthogonal set
concepts.statement: If a vector b is a linear combination of an orthogonal set of vectors w₁, w₂, …, wₙ, then b = (b·w₁)/(w₁·w₁) w₁ + (b·w₂)/(w₂·w₂) w₂ + ⋯ + (b·wₙ)/(wₙ·wₙ) wₙ (Proposition 6.3.4). The weight c₁ is found by dotting both sides of c₁w₁ + c₂w₂ + ⋯ + cₙwₙ = b with w₁ and applying the distributive property of dot products: the presence of an orthogonal set causes most of the terms in the sum to vanish, leaving c₁w₁·w₁ = b·w₁, and in the same way cᵢ = (b·wᵢ)/(wᵢ·wᵢ). In the past we wrote a vector as a linear combination of basis vectors by solving a linear system; the task is simplified when the basis vectors are orthogonal to each other.

forms.condition: b a linear combination of the orthogonal set w₁, w₂, …, wₙ

concepts.name: An orthogonal set is linearly independent
concepts.statement: An orthogonal set of vectors w₁, w₂, …, wₙ is linearly independent (Proposition 6.3.5). If one of the vectors were a linear combination of the others, say w₃ = c₁w₁ + c₂w₂, we would know that w₃ = (w₃·w₁)/(w₁·w₁) w₁ + (w₃·w₂)/(w₂·w₂) w₂ = 0, which cannot happen since w₃ is nonzero.

forms.condition: if w₃ were a linear combination of w₁ and w₂

concepts.name: Orthogonal basis
concepts.statement: If the vectors in an orthogonal set have dimension m, they form a linearly independent set in ℝᵐ and are therefore a basis for the subspace W = Span{w₁, w₂, …, wₙ}; if there are m vectors in the orthogonal set, they form a basis for ℝᵐ. We call a basis orthogonal if the basis vectors are orthogonal to one another.

concepts.name: Unit vector
concepts.statement: A vector having length 1 is called a unit vector. We may multiply any nonzero vector w by a scalar so that the new vector has length 1: if s is a positive scalar, then |sw| = s|w|.

concepts.name: Scaling a vector to unit length
concepts.statement: To obtain a vector u having unit length parallel to a nonzero vector w, we want |u| = |sw| = s|w| = 1, so that s = 1/|w|. Therefore u = (1/|w|) w becomes a unit vector parallel to w: from w₁ = [1, −1, 1], with |w₁| = √3, we find u₁ = [1/√3, −1/√3, 1/√3].

concepts.name: Orthonormal set
concepts.statement: An orthonormal set is an orthogonal set of vectors each of which has unit length. Orthogonal sets in which the vectors have unit length are especially convenient.

concepts.name: Orthonormal basis
concepts.statement: The vectors u₁ = [1/√2, 1/√2] and u₂ = [−1/√2, 1/√2] are an orthonormal set of vectors in ℝ² and form an orthonormal basis for ℝ². Given an orthogonal basis of a subspace, we may scale each vector appropriately to produce an orthonormal basis.

concepts.name: QᵀQ for orthonormal columns
concepts.statement: If the columns of the m × n matrix Q form an orthonormal set, then QᵀQ = Iₙ, the n × n identity matrix (Proposition 6.3.8), because this product computes the dot products between the columns of Q: for Q = [u₁ u₂], QᵀQ = [u₁·u₁ u₁·u₂; u₂·u₁ u₂·u₂] = [1 0; 0 1].

forms.condition: the columns of the m × n matrix Q an orthonormal set

forms.latex: Q^TQ = \begin{bmatrix} {\mathbf u}_1\cdot{\mathbf u}_1 & {\mathbf u}_1\cdot{\mathbf u}_2 \\ {\mathbf u}_2\cdot{\mathbf u}_1 & {\mathbf u}_2\cdot{\mathbf u}_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}

concepts.name: Orthogonality gives the closest vector
concepts.statement: Given a line L in ℝ² defined by the vector w and a vector b not on the line, the vector b̂ on the line closest to b is found by requiring that b − b̂ be orthogonal to L. If y is another vector on the line, then the Pythagorean theorem implies that |b − y|² = |b − b̂|² + |b̂ − y|², which means that |b − y| ≥ |b − b̂|; therefore b̂ is closer to b than any other vector on the line L.

forms.latex: \left|{\mathbf b}-{\mathbf y}\right|^2 = |{\mathbf b}-\widehat{{\mathbf b}}|^2 + |\widehat{{\mathbf b}}-{\mathbf y}|^2
forms.condition: y another vector on the line L, b − b̂ orthogonal to L

concepts.name: Orthogonal projection
concepts.statement: Given a vector b in ℝᵐ and a subspace W of ℝᵐ, the orthogonal projection of b onto W is the vector b̂ in W that is closest to b, meaning the distance between b̂ and b is as small as possible. It is characterized by the property that b − b̂ is orthogonal to W: (b − b̂)·w = 0 for any vector w in W.

forms.condition: for any vector w in W

concepts.name: Orthogonal projection onto a line
concepts.statement: The orthogonal projection of b onto the line defined by w is b̂ = (b·w)/(w·w) w. Since b̂ = sw for some scalar s and b − sw is orthogonal to w, the dot product (b − sw)·w = 0, and the distributive property of dot products gives s = (b·w)/(w·w); for w = [2, 1] and b = [2, 4], b̂ = [16/5, 8/5].

forms.latex: \widehat{{\mathbf b}}= \frac{{\mathbf b}\cdot{\mathbf w}}{{\mathbf w}\cdot{\mathbf w}}~{\mathbf w}

concepts.name: Projection formula
concepts.statement: If W is a subspace of ℝᵐ having an orthogonal basis w₁, w₂, …, wₙ and b is a vector in ℝᵐ, then the orthogonal projection of b onto W is b̂ = (b·w₁)/(w₁·w₁) w₁ + (b·w₂)/(w₂·w₂) w₂ + ⋯ + (b·wₙ)/(wₙ·wₙ) wₙ (Proposition 6.3.15, the projection formula). Writing b̂ = c₁w₁ + c₂w₂ + ⋯ + cₙwₙ and requiring (b − b̂)·wᵢ = 0 gives b·wᵢ = cᵢwᵢ·wᵢ, so cᵢ = (b·wᵢ)/(wᵢ·wᵢ). The formula applies only when the basis of W is orthogonal. If u₁, u₂, …, uₙ is an orthonormal basis for W, it simplifies to b̂ = (b·u₁)u₁ + (b·u₂)u₂ + ⋯ + (b·uₙ)uₙ.

forms.condition: w₁, w₂, …, wₙ an orthogonal basis of W

forms.condition: u₁, u₂, …, uₙ an orthonormal basis of W

concepts.name: Projection matrix
concepts.statement: If u₁, u₂, …, uₙ is an orthonormal basis for a subspace W of ℝᵐ, then the matrix transformation that projects vectors in ℝᵐ orthogonally onto W is represented by the matrix P = QQᵀ, where Q = [u₁ u₂ … uₙ] (Proposition 6.3.16): b̂ = (b·u₁)u₁ + ⋯ + (b·uₙ)uₙ = [u₁ u₂ … uₙ][u₁·b; u₂·b; …; uₙ·b] = QQᵀb. For the plane W of Example 6.3.17, QQᵀ = [29/45 4/9 8/45; 4/9 4/9 −2/9; 8/45 −2/9 41/45], and Col(P) = W, so that rank(P) = dim W.

forms.condition: Q = [u₁ u₂ … uₙ], an orthonormal basis of W

concepts.name: Decomposition into a projection and its complement
concepts.statement: If W is a subspace of ℝⁿ with orthogonal complement W⊥, then any n-dimensional vector b can be uniquely written as b = b̂ + b⊥ where b̂ is in W and b⊥ is in W⊥ (Proposition 6.3.18). The vector b̂ is the orthogonal projection of b onto W and b⊥ = b − b̂, which is orthogonal to W, is the orthogonal projection of b onto W⊥.

forms.condition: b̂ in W, b⊥ in W⊥

concepts.name: When a matrix with orthonormal columns is invertible
concepts.statement: If Q is a matrix whose columns u₁, u₂, …, uₙ form an orthonormal set in ℝᵐ, then QᵀQ = Iₙ, because this product computes the dot products between the columns of Q, and QQᵀ is the matrix that projects vectors orthogonally onto W, the subspace spanned by u₁, …, uₙ; matrix multiplication depends on the order. Because QᵀQ = I, there is a temptation to say that Q is invertible, but an invertible matrix must be square, and Q is square only if n = m. In that case W is ℝᵐ, so QQᵀb, the closest vector in ℝᵐ to b, must be b itself: QQᵀ = I, and Q is invertible. A 3 × 2 matrix Q with orthonormal columns has QᵀQ = I₂ and QQᵀ projecting onto a plane, but is not square and cannot be invertible.

forms.condition: n = m, so that W = ℝᵐ

concepts.name: Orthogonal matrix
concepts.statement: A square m × m matrix Q whose columns form an orthonormal basis for ℝᵐ is called orthogonal. This terminology can be a little confusing: we call a basis orthogonal if the basis vectors are orthogonal to one another, but a matrix is orthogonal if the columns are orthogonal to one another and have unit length.

concepts.name: Inverse of an orthogonal matrix
concepts.statement: An orthogonal matrix Q is invertible and its inverse is Q⁻¹ = Qᵀ (Proposition 6.3.23): since QᵀQ = I and QQᵀ = I, finding the inverse of Q is as simple as writing its transpose. The 3 × 3 matrix whose columns are u₁ = [1/√3, −1/√3, 1/√3], u₂ = [1/√2, 1/√2, 0], u₃ = [1/√6, −1/√6, −2/√6] is orthogonal.

concepts.name: Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization
concepts.statement: Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization begins with a basis v₁, v₂, …, vₙ for a subspace W of ℝᵐ and produces an orthogonal basis w₁, w₂, …, wₙ for W: w₁ = v₁, w₂ = v₂ − (v₂·w₁)/(w₁·w₁) w₁, w₃ = v₃ − (v₃·w₁)/(w₁·w₁) w₁ − (v₃·w₂)/(w₂·w₂) w₂, and so on, each wⱼ being vⱼ minus its orthogonal projection onto the subspace spanned by the earlier vectors. The algorithm relies on our construction of the orthogonal projection, which formed b̂ by requiring that b − b̂ be orthogonal to W, for this allows us to create a vector that is orthogonal to a given subspace. From here, an orthonormal basis is formed by constructing a unit vector parallel to each vector in the orthogonal basis, uⱼ = (1/|wⱼ|) wⱼ. Applied to a linearly dependent set, the algorithm produces a zero vector and fails to give a basis.

concepts.name: Gram-Schmidt preserves the span
concepts.statement: At each step of Gram-Schmidt, the new vectors span the same subspace as the old: Span{w₁, w₂, …, wⱼ} = Span{v₁, v₂, …, vⱼ}. In Example 6.4.4, w₂ = v₂ + w₁, so v₂ = −w₁ + w₂ and any linear combination c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ = c₁w₁ + c₂(−w₁ + w₂) = (c₁ − c₂)w₁ + c₂w₂ is a linear combination of w₁ and w₂; this tells us that W₂ = Span{w₁, w₂} = Span{v₁, v₂}, so w₁ and w₂ are an orthogonal basis for W₂, the 2-dimensional subspace that is the span of v₁ and v₂, and finally Span{w₁, w₂, w₃} = Span{v₁, v₂, v₃}, a new orthogonal basis for ℝ³.

concepts.name: QR factorization
concepts.statement: If A is an m × n matrix whose columns are linearly independent, we may write A = QR where Q is an m × n matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis for Col(A) and R is an n × n upper triangular matrix (Proposition 6.4.5). When the columns of A are linearly independent, they form a basis for Col(A), so we can perform the Gram-Schmidt algorithm, and writing each column of A as a linear combination of the orthonormal basis gives the columns of R. The value of the QR factorization becomes clear in solving least-squares problems.

forms.condition: the columns of A linearly independent; Q m × n with orthonormal columns, R n × n upper triangular

concepts.name: Finding a QR factorization
concepts.statement: To find the QR factorization of A = [v₁ v₂ v₃], apply Gram-Schmidt to the columns to obtain the orthogonal basis w₁, w₂, w₃ and the orthonormal basis u₁, u₂, u₃; since wⱼ = |wⱼ|uⱼ, each column is a combination of the uⱼ. In Example 6.4.6, v₁ = w₁ = 3u₁, v₂ = −w₁ + w₂ = −3u₁ + 3u₂ and v₃ = −w₁ + 2w₂ + w₃ = −3u₁ + 6u₂ + 3u₃, so with Q = [u₁ u₂ u₃] we have A = Q[3 −3 −3; 0 3 6; 0 0 3] = QR. The jth column rⱼ of R holds the weights with Qrⱼ = vⱼ, and R is upper triangular because vⱼ involves only u₁, …, uⱼ.
